en: The *Bhikṣu-śīla-mūla-saṃgraha* with Explanatory Notes, Volume One,
from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (the "Dharmaguptaka" [Tánwúdé] school, translated into Chinese as "Fǎhù").
Bowing my head in worship to all Buddhas, as well as to the Dharma and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, I now expound the Vinaya-dharma.
To cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time:
The precepts are like a boundless ocean; like jewels, one seeks them without satiety. Desiring to protect the noble wealth of the Dharma, you assembly, gather and listen as I speak.
To eliminate the four *pārājika* rules and extinguish the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, To obstruct the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules— May the assembly gather and listen as I speak.
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni—
these World-Honored Ones of great virtue have explained this matter for me;
I now wish to explain it well, so may all you worthy ones listen together.
Just as a person whose feet are injured is unable to travel anywhere, so it is with one who has violated the precepts: they cannot be reborn among gods or humans.
If you wish to be born in the heavens, or if you wish to be born among humans, you must always guard the feet of your precepts so that they remain unimpaired.
Just as a driver entering a perilous path feels anxiety when he loses a pin or breaks an axle, so it is with one who violates the precepts; at the time of death, they shall harbor fear.

Just as a person looking into a mirror feels joy or grief at their own beauty or ugliness, so it is with the recitation of the precepts: one experiences sorrow or delight according to whether they are fully observed or violated.
As when two armies engage in battle, The brave advance while the timid retreat, So it is with the recitation of the precepts:
The pure feel peace, while the defiled feel fear.
Among all the stars, the moon is supreme; Among all the sages, the Buddha is supreme; Among all the various codes of discipline, [The Prātimokṣa is supreme.]
"The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is the supreme and most excellent;
the Tathāgata established these prohibitions and recites them every half-month.

The preceding verses were composed by the Venerable Dharmarakṣa as a general preface for both the extensive and abbreviated versions of the teaching. They first introduce the discourse on observing and violating [the precepts], thereby establishing the foundation for the exposition and the audience.
From "Harmony" (*sāmagrī*) onwards, the main body of the two teachings is divided into three parts:
the Introduction, the Main Teaching, and the Dissemination.
What is "Harmony"?
At that time, there were those who shared the same teacher but belonged to different groups and recited the precepts separately.
The rule was that they ought to respect and serve one another, honor the *poṣadha*, and dwell together in harmony to recite the precepts;
those who violated this were to be charged with an offense.
The Buddha said, "There are three kinds of concordance:
first, those who ought to come do come;
second, those who ought to give their consent (chanda) do give their consent."
3. Those who are present and entitled to censure do not censure;
conversely, this constitutes a separate assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*).
Is the Saṃgha assembled?

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, remained within the boundary (sīmā) or at a site for the precept platform (sīmaṇḍala), yet did not go to the place where the recitation was to be held.
The Buddha said:
"One should seek him out; one should summon him. This is my instruction."
If one goes outside the boundary, or goes there but does not sit [in the assembly], one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

From this day forward, wherever there is even a single bhikṣu, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, he should first go to the poṣadha hall, sweep and sprinkle it, arrange the seats, prepare water, light lamps, and set out the śalākā (voting sticks), and so forth.
If guests arrive, whether there are four or more, the *pāṭimokkha* should be recited;
even if there is but one person, they should maintain mental purity.
If there are those who perform an unlawful separate assembly for the recitation of the precepts, they must be dealt with according to the Dharma.

When those who had not yet received full ordination departed, there was a bhikṣu who caused others to obstruct the recitation of the precepts; the Buddha then ordered them all to go to a place where they could neither see nor hear [the proceedings].
It is permissible for others who have not yet received the precepts or non-human beings to come;
furthermore, one should not perform this in the presence of nuns.
"Which bhikṣus who have not come have declared their *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*?
At the time of the *poṣadha*, there may be a sick bhikṣu, or one tending to the sick, or one occupied with matters concerning the Triple Gem, who does not come to hear the recitation of the precepts.
The Buddha said:
"One should grant the consent (*chanda*) and the purification (*pāriśuddhi*), according to whether they are extensive or concise.
If one neither manifests the physical signs nor speaks with the mouth, it is not accomplished."
If the illness is severe, one should ascend into the midst of the Saṃgha;
however, fearing that the illness might worsen or cause agitation, one may perform the rite outside the boundary.
This is because there is no expedient means by which one may perform a *jñapti-karman* for a separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*) to recite the precepts.
“Whom has the community of bhikṣuṇīs sent?
The Buddha said,
“If there is anyone [sent], one should immediately rise and say:”
“The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha is in harmony; we pay homage at the feet of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha.
This is explained in detail in the *Śānbù Jíemó* (Supplemented and Revised Karma-vastu).
If no one comes, he should reply:
"There are no nuns to request instruction.
Now that the Saṃgha is in harmony, what should be done?
He should answer:
Regarding the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts, the Buddha said:
"On the day of the recitation of the precepts, one must not remain in one's private room."
Regarding the mutual inspection of the seats to determine whether anyone has arrived or not:
one should first make an announcement, and only then recite the precepts.
If a foolish bhikṣu says, "I did not recite it before," or if someone has forgotten [a portion], the recitation of the precepts is not valid.
One should rely on those capable of reciting the precepts.
A bhikṣu with five years of seniority should recite them until they are mastered.

If one goes to a nearby location to study the introduction to the precepts and even other teachings, upon returning to one's own place, one should explain them in sequence and need not recite them again.
"If you cannot obtain it, simply preach the Dharma and recite the sūtras, then rise from your seats.
Otherwise, you shall be dealt with according to the law. Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha performs the uposatha and recites the precepts.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the uposatha be performed and the precepts be recited.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The Buddha said:
"One should follow the king’s reckoning, whether it be the fourteenth day or the fifteenth day.
One should employ the method of counting, wherein there are fifteen days each for both the dark fortnight and the bright fortnight."
Follow the precedent of Candragomin:
if four persons are present, one should perform this formal announcement (*jñapti*);
if three or fewer, the precepts should be recited with a threefold proclamation.
"Venerable sirs!
I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa.
The Buddha said:
"Those who have newly received the precepts have not yet heard them and do not know what they should train in; let them gather in one place and recite them together in harmony.
The *Prātimokṣa* is the precept."
It is because one maintains dignified deportment and one’s dwelling place, cultivates the faculties and the countenance, gathers all wholesome dharmas, and achieves samādhi;
and because one should bind [the mudrās], should speak [the mantras], should initiate [the practice], and should extensively expound, reveal, and repeatedly analyze them.
The bhikṣus gathered together in one place.
The Buddha said:
"Those who share the same *karmavācanā* gather in one place; even until those who ought to be rebuked do not rebuke [the offender], this is called acting according to the Dharma."
If the assembly is large and the voices are faint, one should arrange an exquisite high seat and preach while standing upon it.
In cases of the eight difficulties or other circumstances, one may preach briefly according to the occasion.
If guests and residents gather together in small or large numbers, once this introduction has been delivered, one should announce that the area is purified and then allow them to listen.
The remainder is as detailed in the *Vinaya*.
Listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
The Buddha said:
One should listen to the Dharma with a focused mind and single-minded intent.
If one knows for oneself that one has committed an offense, one should immediately perform repentance.
The Buddha said:
"It refers to the fact that the offense committed has not yet been confessed.
There are two kinds of wise persons:
those who recognize their transgressions when they have committed them, and those who, having recognized their transgressions, confess them according to the Dharma."
If one wishes to repent, one should approach a pure bhikṣu and declare the name of the offense; once it has been removed according to the Dharma, one may then hear the precepts.
This same procedure applies even when there is doubt regarding an offense.

"If the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense and there is no one available to perform the confession, then regardless of whether it was intentional or suspected, one shall confess by means of a formal announcement (jñapti) and then declare it.
Those who have not committed an offense remain silent.
By remaining silent, it is known that the Venerable Ones are pure.
The Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of those who are without offense:
those who have never committed an offense from the outset, and those who, having committed one, have already repented."
"If others should ask, you should answer in this same way.
The Buddha said:
"It is just as when two bhikṣus question and answer one another."
Thus, when a bhikṣu is among the assembly, if he is asked up to three times and remembers an offense yet does not confess it, he commits a deliberate lie.
Regarding lying, the Buddha has said it is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
The Buddha said:
"Because one commits a silent falsehood when the Sangha recites the precepts, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
As for the phrase "obstructing the Path," it refers to obstructing the four dhyānas, the three emptinesses, and the four fruits [of the śramaṇa].
He addressed the bhikṣus:
“Just as that great ocean does not tolerate a corpse, but if one is present, it washes it out;
so too is my Dharma, which does not tolerate a corpse.”

What is called a "corpse" refers to one who is not a śramaṇa practicing the holy life, yet claims to be a śramaṇa practicing the holy life; one who violates the precepts with evil and impure dharmas, defiled by false views and concealing them, rotten within while appearing whole and pure without, like a tree in the sky;
though sitting among the assembly, he is always far removed from the assembly, and the assembly likewise distances itself from him.
Thus, one knows that the confession of offenses is the very means by which the precepts are heard and realized.
If a bhikṣu remembers having committed an offense and desires to seek purity, he should perform confession; through confession, he shall attain peace and happiness.
The Buddha said:
"By means of training in the pure precepts, one attains pure concentration and wisdom; this is called attaining dhyāna and its fruits, which constitutes 'peaceful bliss.'"
Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Now I ask the venerable sirs:
"Is there purity herein? This is asked three times.
"Venerable sirs!"
In this matter, they are pure because they remain silent.
Thus shall this be upheld.
From this point forward, [the text] constitutes the specific introduction to the "Extensive Teaching" (Vaipulya-śikṣā).
The text that follows is the authentic core of the "Extensive Teaching.
O Venerable Ones!
These four *pārājika* dharmas are recited every half-month; they have come down from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
First, the precept against great sexual misconduct.
When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Vaiśālī,
at that time, Sudinna, having left the household life out of faith, later returned to his native village and engaged in unchaste conduct with his former wife.
Having examined and understood this, the bhikṣus said:

"Within the pure Dharma of the Tathāgata, one should be free from desire regarding sensual desires; one can sever craving, destroy the nest, eliminate all fetters and bonds, and attain nirvāṇa through the exhaustion of craving."
"How could you have committed such an evil deed?

Having reported the transgression to the Buddha, he immediately assembled the community of monks. Knowing the proper time and that it was appropriate for the matter, and having elicited the offender's own confession, the Buddha rebuked him, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the way of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the Dharma; it is something that should not have been done.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"By means of countless skillful methods, I have taught the dharma for severing desire and transcending the fetters of craving."
Furthermore, it is said that this desire is like fire, like a torch, and even like a sword or a halberd.
Having thus rebuked him, [the Buddha declared]: "This is a foolish person; having committed many kinds of outflows, he is the first to violate the precepts."
Now I shall establish the precepts, gathering ten points of meaning:
first, to bring the Sangha together;
second, to cause the Sangha to rejoice;
Third, to bring peace and happiness to the Saṃgha;
fourth, to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed;
fifth, to cause the increase of faith in those who already believe.
Sixth, those who are difficult to tame are tamed and made compliant;
seventh, those with a sense of shame and remorse find peace and happiness;
eighth, one cuts off the outflows (*āsrava*) of the present existence.
"Ninth, the severing of future outflows;
tenth, the long endurance of the True Dharma.
All precepts are likewise; the subsequent ones are abbreviated hereafter.
One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu"— as the Buddha said— refers to a bhikṣu by name,

a bhikṣu in appearance, a bhikṣu by self-claim, a bhikṣu by mendicancy, a bhikṣu by wearing the cut-and-sewn robes, a bhikṣu by having destroyed the fetters (*saṃyojana*), a bhikṣu by the "Come, O Bhikṣu" [invitation], or a bhikṣu who has received full ordination through a formal act of motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) in accordance with the Dharma and attained the status of a monk.

In this context, "bhikṣu" refers to one who has received the full ordination through a formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) in accordance with the Dharma, has attained the status [of a monk], and abides within the discipline of a bhikṣu; such is the meaning of "bhikṣu."
Regarding "together with bhikṣus," the Buddha said:

"If one has received the full ordination together with other bhikṣus through the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and even dwells within the dharma of the bhikṣus—this is the meaning of 'together with bhikṣus'."
Regarding "common precepts" (*sādhāraṇa-śīla*), the Buddha said:
"Once I have established these precepts for my disciples, they would rather die than violate them.
Among them, that which is shared with other bhikṣus—being a common, identical, and equal precept—is what is meant by the meaning of 'common precepts'."
"If he does not return the precepts," the Buddha said,
"if there is a bhikṣu who no longer delights in the holy life (brahmacarya), he is permitted to relinquish the precepts and return home.
If he later wishes to go forth again and cultivate the holy life within the Buddha-dharma, he should be ordained and may receive full ordination (upasampadā)."
Why is it not called "renouncing the precepts"?

If one renounces them while oneself is insane, mentally deranged, afflicted by pain, mute, or deaf; or if one renounces them in the presence of such persons, or in the presence of people from central or peripheral regions who do not share the same understanding, the renunciation is not accomplished.

If one acts in jest, or while asleep, or in the presence of an ignorant person, or does not speak for oneself, or if the person before one does not understand, in all such cases, the renunciation is not accomplished.

If one says, "I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Sangha, the Preceptor, and the Vinaya," or "I accept the household dharma," and so forth, this is called "renouncing the precepts."
Regarding "being weak in the precepts yet not repenting," the Buddha said:
"What is meant by being weak in the precepts yet not relinquishing them?

If there is a bhikṣu who constantly harbors sorrow and anxiety, who does not delight in the holy life (brahmacarya), who grows weary of the dharma of a bhikṣu, and whose mind desires to live as a householder, he says: 'I think of my parents, wife, children, and kinsmen; of villages, towns, cities, gardens, fields, and family affairs. He says, 'I wish to abandon the Buddha,' and so on, up to 'the matters of training'—this is it."
"If one thinks, 'I now relinquish the precepts,' this is to relinquish them while the precepts have already become weak.
Regarding the commission of impure conduct, the Buddha said:
"This is the dharma of sexual desire."
For a male, there are two passages; for a female, there are three.

Whether entering from a passage into a passage, from a passage into a non-passage, or from a non-passage into a passage; whether it is at the opening, or if it enters completely, or even if it enters as much as the tip of a hair—all these constitute a *pārājika* offense.
...up to "with animals. The Buddha said:
"It refers to those places where sexual intercourse can be performed.
There are three kinds of sexual intercourse:"
Humans, non-humans, and the realm of animals.
Furthermore, there are five types:
women, virgins, hermaphrodites, eunuchs, and men.
If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, approaches a person’s three orifices or two orifices, he commits an offense as soon as he first enters; this remains an offense even if there is an obstruction.

If he approaches one who is asleep, or one who is dead but not yet decomposed, or one who is mostly undecomposed, and engages in sexual intercourse at the three orifices or two orifices, he commits an offense as soon as he first enters; thus it is explained in detail.
If a bhikṣu is led before his enemies and is forcibly made to enter three places or two places:
if he experiences pleasure upon first entering, he commits an offense; if he does not experience pleasure, he does not commit an offense.
The cases of being separated by a barrier or not separated by a barrier are also the same as above.
If an enemy forcibly compels a bhikṣu to engage in unchaste conduct, whether he experiences pleasure or displeasure, and whether there is a barrier or no barrier, it is also as described above.
"This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense. The Buddha said:
"For example, just as a person whose head is severed cannot be restored to life, so it is with a bhikṣu; one who violates this rule no longer constitutes a bhikṣu, and thus he is so named."
If one employs a means with the intent to commit an impure act, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense if successful, and a *sthūlātyaya* offense if unsuccessful.
If one instructs a bhikṣu to perform such an act, the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense if the act is carried out;
if it is not carried out, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Excluding monks and nuns, if other members of the community instruct one another regarding what should or should not be done, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If the corpse is half-decomposed, or entirely decomposed, or if one engages in impure conduct between the bones, or in a hole in the ground or a hole in the mud, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If it is a path, and one perceives it as such, or if one is doubtful, or if one perceives it as not being a path, it is a *pārājika*.
If it is not a path, yet one perceives it as a path, or is doubtful about it being a path, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a pārājika offense;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense, and they are to be expelled.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one was asleep and unconscious, did not experience pleasure, and had no intention of sexual misconduct at all.
There is no offense if it occurred before the precept was established, or if one was insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
"One does not dwell together with them.
The Buddha said,
"There are two kinds of dwelling together:"
"Because one cannot abide in these two matters—identical *karmavācanā* and identical recitation of the precepts—it is called 'not living together' (*asaṃvāsa*).
2. The Precept Against Grand Theft.
The Buddha was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.
There was a monk named Dhanika who sat in meditation in a thatched hut in a secluded place; someone carried it away and built a complete house of baked bricks. The Buddha ordered it to be demolished.

He then falsely proclaimed the King’s edict to seize essential timber; consequently, the king’s ministers and the people rebuked him, saying, "Do not allow him to enter the village, and do not let him settle there again."
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, whereupon the precept was established as above.
"If a bhikṣu" has the same meaning as explained above.
"In a village": there are four kinds of villages.
First, walls on all four sides;
second, a palisade fence;
third, a fence or wall that does not enclose the perimeter.
The fourth is "the four sides," which refers to a house with walls on all four sides.
"A secluded place" refers to a quiet location outside a village. "A place" (*sthāna*) includes: whether it is on the ground or above the ground;

whether one is riding, carrying a load, in the air, or on a rack; whether it is in a village, a forest hermitage (*aranyaka*), or a field; whether it is a specific spot, on a boat, or in water; whether it involves crossing a pass or barrier privately without paying taxes; whether it involves taking another's entrusted goods, or taking water, or willow twigs, or garden fruits, grasses, and trees; whether it involves footless beings, or two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed beings; whether it involves shared property or business, or a mutual agreement, or waiting in ambush, or guarding, or patrolling a road—these are called "places."
It is not given because the other person has not relinquished it.

This is because one perceives it as another's property, perceives it as protected by another, perceives that it has an owner, perceives it as not one's own object, perceives it as not for temporary use, or because there was no mutual consent.
"To take with a thieving mind" means to take with a robber's intent.
There are five kinds:
a darkened mind, a deviant mind, a crooked and perverse mind, a fearful and timid mind, and a mind that constantly intends to steal from others.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of appropriation:
appropriation by determination, appropriation through intimidation, appropriation of entrusted property, appropriation upon sight, and appropriation through reliance.

These refer to cases where one appropriates by relying on the power of friends or relatives, or by means of verbal eloquence and persuasion, deceiving and misleading others to take what is not theirs.

In accordance with the law against taking what is not given, the king established a decree stating, "If one takes five coins, or property worth five coins, the offense shall be punishable by death. The Buddha followed this royal law; thus, he prescribed a grave penalty for theft once the value reached that full amount.
If he becomes a king or attains sovereignty such that he is no longer subject to others;

and if the king, his ministers, or various high officials—who assist the king—should seize him, or kill him, or bind him, or drive him out of the country, saying, "You are a thief! You are a fool! You know nothing! then this bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense. Regarding the term "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
If one obtains goods from various locations and the value of the stolen property is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*;
if there was an attempt, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one takes less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If [the object] is not obtained, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one instructs another to steal, and that person obtains the object, both are guilty of *pārājika*.

If the one who receives the instruction takes a different object, or takes the object from a different location, the taker commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), while the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya* as well.
If one causes another to take an object without the intent to steal, the instructor commits a *pārājika* offense, while the recipient does not commit an offense.
If one instructs another to take an object by commanding them to steal it, the recipient commits a grave offense, while the instructor is without offense.
If there is the perception that an object has an owner, one commits a grave offense (pārājika); if one is in doubt, it is a serious offense (sthūlātyaya).
Regarding an object that has no owner, if one perceives it as having an owner or is in doubt, it is a serious offense.
The four assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs, are all subject to the same precepts as above.

Those who do not commit an offense are those who take with the perception that it belongs to another, the perception that it is their own, the perception that it is refuse-rag material, the perception that they are taking it temporarily, or the perception that the owner is a close friend.
"Not living together.
The meaning is as explained above.
Third, the precept against killing on a large scale.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī and taught the contemplation of impurity to the bhikṣus.
Having practiced this meditation, they came to loathe their bodies and lives, praising death and encouraging one another toward it.
The bhikṣu Nanda had been hired to kill a man, which caused the householder to be struck with terror.
The Buddha, knowing of this matter, then taught the dharma of dhyāna.
The bhikṣu practiced it and together realized the higher fruits of the path.
This precept was established because of the censure of the aforementioned transgressions.

If a bhikṣu intentionally takes life with his own hand—meaning he commits murder—whether he kills himself, causes another to kill, sends a messenger to kill, dispatches a messenger back and forth to kill, sends a subordinate messenger to kill, sends a succession of messengers to kill, seeks out a man to kill, instructs another to seek out a man to kill, seeks out a man with a sword to kill, instructs another to seek out a man with a sword to kill, manifests signs with the body, speaks with the voice, or manifests signs with both body and voice; whether he instructs another to utter praise [of killing], sends a letter, instructs another to send a letter, digs a pitfall, uses a trap, gives poison, provides the means for death, or employs any other such expedient means to kill—this constitutes the offense.
Regarding human life, one cuts off that life from the initial consciousness to the final consciousness.
One hands a blade to another, praises death, and encourages death, saying: "Ho! Man!"
"What is the use of this wretched life?
It is better to die than to live!

Thinking thus and contemplating in various ways, he praises death, extols death, and earnestly encourages death. This bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense. If he employs the aforementioned means to kill another person but the person does not die, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one kills a non-human, or an animal that possesses intelligence, understands human speech, or is capable of transforming its form, and one kills it through skillful means, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it does not die, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one kills an animal that cannot transform its form, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is actually a human being and one perceives them as such, it is a *pārājika*;
if one perceives them as a non-human or has doubt regarding their status, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The characteristics of offenses for the fourfold assembly are as stated above.
Those who do not commit an offense include cases where one throws a blade, a staff, a tile, or a stone, and [the victim] dies by accident.
If one dies while engaged in construction work, such as building a dwelling, by accidentally falling over wood or stone;
or if one dies while assisting a patient, moving back and forth into a room—provided there was no harmful intent in any of these cases—this is it.
Not to live in community [with one who has committed it]. Fourth, the precept against great falsehood.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
