If a bhikṣu leaves his robe within a monastery, or even stays overnight beneath a tree, and before the dawn has appeared, he either relinquishes the robe, holds it in his hand, or reaches a place where a stone could be thrown;

or if he does not relinquish the robe, does not hold it in his hand, and does not reach a place where a stone could be thrown, yet the dawn appears—then according to the distance from which he is separated from the robe, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Except by means of a formal monastic act (*saṃgha-karman*), there was a time when a bhikṣu suffered from the disease of consumption (*śoṣa*). His *saṃghāṭī* made of discarded rags was extremely heavy; having a matter requiring him to travel among the people, he was unable to carry it while traveling. He reported this matter to the Buddha.
If the Buddha has commanded that one must request [permission] three times before departing,
and one departs after making a formal motion and announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*),
it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Apart from the three robes, if one leaves any other garment behind, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Nuns commit the same offenses as monks.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the Saṃgha has performed a formal ritual (karmavācanā); [and so forth].
If the light of dawn has not yet appeared, whether one holds the robe in hand, sets it down, or reaches a place where a stone could be thrown;

or if there is the perception of being robbed, or if the path by water or land is cut off due to urgent distress, or if one is seized by bandits, wild beasts, or the powerful; or if there is danger to life or to one's religious practice (*brahmacarya*)—if, under such circumstances, one does not set down the robe or reach the distance of a stone’s throw, one does not commit an offense.
3. The precept concerning the limit on keeping extra robes beyond the full moon.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu who possessed only the three robes found that his saṃghāṭī had become worn out and he was unable to have it repaired within ten days. Therefore, the Buddha permitted him to keep an extra robe (atireka-cīvara) for the purpose of fulfilling his requirements.
The group of six bhikṣus took robes that were insufficient for them, washed, dyed, and purified them by marking them, and then left them with others while they went traveling.
When other bhikṣus pointed out their transgression, the Buddha rebuked them and established a precept.
If a bhikṣu’s robes are finished and the kaṭhina has been relinquished, and that bhikṣu obtains out-of-season robe-cloth—“season” being, when there is no kaṭhina, one month after the *pravāraṇā*;
when there is a kaṭhina, five months after the *pravāraṇā*.
"Untimely" means exceeding this limit.
If one wishes to receive [the food], one may do so; once received, it is quickly prepared.
If it is sufficient, that is well.
If one's clothing requirements are met within ten days, one should cut and sew them as described above;
otherwise, by the eleventh day, depending on the quantity of cloth, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one lacks sufficient [robes], one may keep them for one month in order to fulfill the requirement.

If one lacks sufficient robes of the same kind, but they become sufficient on the eleventh day, then on that eleventh day one must perform the ritual as described above; otherwise, by the twelfth day, one commits an offense regarding all such robes.
This continues in the same manner up to the twenty-ninth day.
On the thirtieth day, whether the [robe] is complete or incomplete, whether it is the same cloth or different, one shall act on that very day according to the aforementioned rule.
If one keeps [the item] beyond that limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The same offense applies to bhikṣuṇīs. There is no offense in the following cases:
If within ten days one has sufficient cloth to make a robe, or even up to thirty days, one must make the robe that very day;
otherwise, there is a cause for offense, as in the "Rule on Extra Cloth.
Fourth, the rule against accepting robes from a nun who is not a relative.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
The nun Utpalavarṇā took food to the mountain to offer it to the senior elders (*sthavira*).
There was a bhikṣu there wearing a worn-out, tattered robe; the nun took off her own expensive garment and exchanged it for his, subsequently putting on the worn-out robe herself.
The Buddha, being astonished by this, questioned and rebuked that bhikṣu, and consequently established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu [accepts food] from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative—where 'not a relative' means one who is neither a parent nor related within seven generations;
conversely, those above this are relatives."
If they are not relatives, one does not deliberate on whether it is acceptable or not;
if they are relatives, however, one does deliberate, considering whether [the goods] exist or not, whether they may be taken or not, and whether they are good or bad, new or old, and so forth.
Regarding the taking of robes, there are ten kinds of robes.
When a nun wore a worn-out robe, she reported this in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be like this."

It is permitted to keep five robes that are complete and sturdy; as for other robes, they may be given away according to one's will through a formal act of purification (pariṣkāra-dāna) or bestowed upon another.
Why is this? Even when women wear fine garments, they do not appear beautiful, let alone when they wear those that are worn out and old.
"Except for trade, at that time the two divisions of the Saṃgha obtained robes and divided them together; however, the two divisions received each other's shares. The Buddha said:
'I allow you to exchange robes with one another. As for what is called 'trade':"
This refers to trading robes for robes,
or trading what is not a robe for a robe— such as needles, tubes, knives, thread, small items, or even a single pill of medicine— in exchange for a robe.
This constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for a bhikṣuṇī and a *duṣkṛta* for a bhikṣu.
There is no offense if she takes the robe from a relative bhikṣuṇī, or if she obtains it through trade, or if she takes it for the sake of the Saṃgha or for the Buddha’s shrine.
5. The precept against commanding a nun who is not a relative to wash one’s old robes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

Kāḷodāyin and the nun Thullanandā were both handsome; they became mutually infatuated, and while sitting together, they emitted impurity, which soiled his *antarvāsaka* (undergarment). He then ordered the nun to wash it for him.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who, after rebuking them, established the rule:
"If a bhikṣu causes a person who is not a relative—as described above—to [wash, dye, or beat] [a robe], he commits an offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a non-relative śikṣamāṇā or śrāmaṇerī to wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
To wash an old garment: "old garment" refers to one that has been worn on the body at least once.
To wash, dye, or beat a new garment constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one dyes or beats it oneself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. If one instructs another to wash, dye, or beat it, or if one performs all three actions oneself, there are three *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.
If one does not perform these duties for one another, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense for each instance.
There is no offense if, when ill, one causes [another] to wash, dye, or beat [the robes];
or if it is for the sake of the Saṃgha or a Buddhist monastery; or if one borrows another's robe and then washes, dyes, or beats it.
6. The precept against begging for robes from a layperson who is not a relative.
When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time, Upananda preached the Dharma for someone and asked them for the robe they were wearing.
After a brief interval, he entered the city wearing only a single robe and immediately declared,
"The Jetavana has been plundered by bandits.
The laypeople mocked and disparaged him.
When the monks reported this transgression, the Buddha then established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu requests a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, the explanation of the details is as above."
Except at other times, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The same offense applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
As for "other times": if one's robes have been taken away, or if a bhikṣu has had his robes stripped by bandits and is walking about naked—the Buddha said:
"No; one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If such [a robe] exists, one should cover one's body with soft grass or tree leaves and go to the vicinity of the monastery; one may take it from there, or if it is too long, one may take it from a friend.
If none is available, one should ask within the Saṃgha for a portionable robe."
If there is nothing [in the storehouse], one should ask for monastic robes or bedding;

if they are not given, one may personally open the storehouse to look. If there are mats, rugs, felt, or blankets, one may tear them apart, cut them, and make them into robes, then go outside to beg for clothing.
"If, having obtained the robe, one returns it to wash, dye, and mend it, and places it back in its original location;
if one does not return it to its original location, it shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
The circumstances regarding the loss of a robe, the burning of a robe, or the drifting away of a robe are the same as above.
This is called "other occasions.
There is no offense in cases such as when one begs from a non-relative due to circumstances such as being robbed or losing [the item].
Whether begging from a relative,
begging from a renunciant,
or begging on behalf of another;
If he begs for it himself, or obtains it without having asked, there is no offense.
Seventh: The precept against taking clothing in excess.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Many bhikṣus encountered bandits and lost their robes; they came to the Jetavana.
Hearing of this, many faithful people sent them many robes. The bhikṣus said:
"Stop; you have already made an offering.
Since you possess the three robes, there is no need for this.
The group of six monks insisted that he take it, saying, "Take it and give it to us."
He then accepted them again.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and the Buddha consequently established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu loses his robe, has it seized, has it burned, or has it washed away—if he loses even one robe—he should not accept [another]."
If two robes are lost and the remaining two robes are double, triple, or quadruple-layered, one should tear them to make a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, or an antarvāsaka.
If it is a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative, they are both to be understood as explained above.

If one is invited at the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and given much clothing, whether the clothing be fine, thin, or not durable, one should take it and make it double, triple, or quadruple-layered; one should add borders and make them, fold the soiled areas over the shoulders, and provide hooks and fasteners.
If there is any remainder, one should say to those of higher status, "What shall this remaining robe-material be made into?
If the donor says, "I did not give this because my robes were lost; we gave it to you, Venerable Sir, of our own accord," then if one wishes to accept it, one should do so.
This bhikṣu should receive robes with contentment.
If his three robes are all lost, he should receive robes with contentment.
There are two kinds of contentment:
For laypeople who are content, they accept whatever robes are given by householders;
for renunciants who are content, it is the three robes (*tricīvara*).
To exceed this means that if one robe is lost, one must receive another, following the rule that if all three are lost, all three must be received again.
This is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The same offense applies to a bhikṣuṇī. There is no offense in the following cases:
If one takes robes knowing one’s own sufficiency;
if one takes less than what is sufficient;

if more robes are offered that are fine, thin, or not durable; or if they are made in two or three layers and there is a surplus—provided one knows these matters as described above—one does not commit an offense.
8. The Precept Against Encouraging a Householder to Increase the Price of Robes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A householder and his wife were discussing together, saying:
“Bhadananda is an old friend of mine; take this price for robes and buy a garment to give him.
When the bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard this, he informed [the donor].
Later, he went to that house and urged them that the robe must be vast, new, fine, and sturdy.
Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, and the bhikṣus reported their transgressions.
The Buddha then established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu [acts as described] with a householder or a householder’s wife, as stated above..."
To provide the price for robes for a bhikṣu means to use either money, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, jade, ornaments, raw or wrought gold, or even the ten kinds of cloth.

"If one possesses such a price for robes and gives them to a certain bhikṣu," if that bhikṣu has not previously accepted an invitation to choose at will, and if [the donor] asks at will, "What kind of robe do you require?"—the Buddha permits the bhikṣu, being of few desires and contented, to seek one that is inferior.
Having gone to the house of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*), one speaks thus: "Excellent, lay devotee!
Buy such a robe for me and give it to me, so that it may be of good quality. There are two kinds of seeking:
as for "seeking the price," it refers to when a donor provides a robe of great value, even to the extent of seeking an increase of one-sixteenth part of a single coin.
Regarding the phrase "seeking robes," it means saying to a layperson, "Make a robe wide and long," or even adding a single thread [to its dimensions].
If one obtains such a robe, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to the offense for a bhikṣuṇī. There is no offense in the following cases:
if one goes to seek [food] after having previously accepted an invitation for a *pravāraṇā* feast; if one is content with what is obtained; or if one reduces the amount requested during the search.
Seeking from relatives;
seeking from those who have left the household life;
or seeking on behalf of another.
He seeks it for himself;
or if he obtains it without seeking.
Ninth, the precept against encouraging two families to increase the price of robes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There were two laypeople, a husband and wife, who consulted together, intending to purchase robes for Upananda.
When the bhikṣu who went on alms-round heard of this, he reported it in full to the Buddha.
He went to two households and told them to work together.
The laypeople criticized and disparaged him, and the bhikṣus reported his transgression.
Consequently, the Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.

If a bhikṣu, when two householders or a householder’s wife have prepared the price for a robe for him, saying, "Buy such a robe and give it to this bhikṣu," and that bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation to choose [the robe], goes to the houses of those two householders and speaks thus: "Excellent, householders!..."
"If you provide the price for such a robe and we make one robe together for the sake of its excellence," if she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The characteristics of the offense and its exemptions are as in the preceding precepts.
Tenth: The precept against demanding clothing beyond the limit.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A high minister of Rājagṛha was on intimate terms with Upananda and used to send him the price for robes.
Having entrusted that money for robes to a designated custodian, he later urgently demanded it back due to pressing business, which resulted in the custodian being punished.
The laypeople criticized and disparaged them, and the bhikṣus reported these transgressions.
Consequently, the Buddha established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu [should serve] a king who possesses sovereign power and is not subject to anyone else..."
If they are ministers, they are those who stand at the king's side.
If they are brahmins, they are those born into the brahmin caste.
If they are householders—excluding kings, ministers, and brahmins—they are all those who live as laypeople.
A householder’s wife refers to a woman living at home.
She sends a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a bhikṣu, as described above, saying:
"Take this price for a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu."
That messenger went to where the bhikṣu was and said to him:
"Venerable sir!
For your sake, this price for a robe has been sent; please accept it."
That bhikṣu should speak thus to the messenger:
"I ought not to accept this price for robes.
If I require robes, I shall accept them at the proper time and in a pure manner."
The messenger said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir, is there anyone who attends to the affairs [of the Saṃgha]?"
The bhikṣu should say: "There is.
Whether he be a monastery attendant (ārāmika) or an upāsaka, this person is a steward for the bhikṣus and constantly attends to their affairs."
Then that messenger went to the person in charge, gave him the price for the robe, and returned to the bhikṣu, speaking thus:
"Venerable sir, I have already given the price for the robe to the person in charge whom you designated."
"Venerable sir, you know the proper time; go there and you shall obtain robes.
A bhikṣu who requires robes should go to the person in charge of affairs and, after reminding them a second or third time, should say:
"I require robes."

Regarding "one who reminds": whether it be an attendant, a householder, one in the marketplace, or one at a place of labor, one should go to that person's location and say once, twice, or three times: "I now require robes; please make them for me. This is what is meant.
If, after reminding him a second or third time, he obtains the robe, that is well.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should stand silently before him for a fourth, fifth, and sixth time.
That attendant, whether at home, in the market, or at his place of work, should stand silently before him.
The attendant asks:
"For what reason do you stand here?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"You should know for yourself.
If that person says:
"If I do not know now, and there are others who do know, the bhikṣus should say:
'That person knows it.'"
This is the sign of silence.
If one remains silent before [the assembly] for four, five, or six times, it is well if one obtains the robe.
If one speaks once, it breaks two instances of silence; up to the point that speaking three times breaks six instances of silence.
If she does not obtain the robe, and after this [period] she seeks to obtain a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This offense applies equally to monks and nuns.
If she does not obtain the robe, she may go herself or send a messenger to the place where the price for the robe was obtained and say:
"You previously sent a messenger with the price for robes to give to a certain bhikṣu, but that bhikṣu did not ultimately receive the robes.
You should go back and retrieve them; do not let them be lost."
This is the proper time. There is no offense if he informs by means of a messenger;
or if that person says, "I do not need this now, I shall give it to you as a gift," and the bhikṣu then seeks the robe at the proper time, with gentle speech, and through skillful means.

If one receives [cotton] for the purpose of making a *pālikara* (a small pillow or bolster), and having requested it at the proper time with gentle words, or having obtained it through skillful means—
this is the eleventh precept concerning the bedding made of cotton.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kalandaka.

The group of six bhikṣus went to the house of a silkworm raiser and requested raw silk that had not yet been processed, as well as processed silk, along with wild silk, to make bedding; they also watched the boiling of cocoons.
The laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying, "They take life; there is no true Dharma here.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and because of it, the Buddha established the precept:
If a bhikṣu mixes wool, cotton, cloth, or other fibers [to make a rug].

Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for making a new bedding from wild silkworm cotton that must be relinquished: if it is an axe or a hatchet, one should chop and hack it, mix it with clay, and use it to plaster a wall.
It is a *pāyattika*.
Whether one acts oneself or instructs another, if it is accomplished, both are guilty;
if it is not accomplished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes another to do it and it is completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if one obtains what has already been made and uses an axe to chop it into pieces to mix with mud for plastering the wall-base.
12. The Precept on Black Woolen Bedding.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
Many Licchavi youths engaged in illicit conduct; they made black woolen blankets and wore them while walking about at night so that people would not see them.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw this, they intentionally did it again, which the Licchavis criticized and disparaged.
The bhikṣus reported the matter, and the Buddha consequently established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu uses new cloth that is purely black, or naturally black, or dyed black..."
To make a new bedding or mat from the wool of a ram constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Whether one does it oneself, instructs another, or has it done for oneself, the characteristics of the transgression are the same as in the preceding precept.
A nun commits a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if she obtains one that is already completed.
If it is cut or torn;
if it is made of thin material folded double;
or if it is a small sitting mat.
Whether making a mattress, a hat, or a robe;
Using it as a towel for wiping sweat, or using it as a cloth for wrapping leather sandals—in all such cases, there is no offense.
Thirteen: The precept concerning bedding made of white hair.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The group of six bhikṣus made new bedding exclusively from white wool, which the householders criticized and disparaged, saying, "They are just like kings and high ministers."
When the monks reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently rebuked them and established a rule:
"If a monk makes a new bedding, he should use two parts of pure black wool, and three parts of white wool, either naturally white or dyed white."
The variegated [wool] consists of hair from the head, hair from the ears, hair from the legs, or any other variegated-colored wool.
One who wishes to make a bedding of forty *patra* should use twenty *patra* of black, ten *patra* of white, and ten *patra* of variegated wool.
This applies even up to making twenty *pātra* worth of bedding; it may be understood by analogy with what was stated above.
If a bhikṣu makes new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether one makes it oneself, instructs another to do so, or has someone else make it for oneself, all are treated as above.
For a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if it is made according to the proper measure, or if one obtains what has already been completed; the rest is the same as the preceding precept.
14. The Precept on Reducing Bedding by Six Years.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

The group of six bhikṣus, dissatisfied with their old bedding—whether it was too heavy or too light, too thick or too thin—did not discard the old items but instead made new ones; they constantly sought after them and accumulated many in store.
When the monks reported this transgression, the Buddha rebuked them and established a precept:
If a monk makes a new bedding or mat, he must use it for six years.

If it is less than six years and he makes another new one without relinquishing the old, whether he does so himself, instructs another to do so, or acts on behalf of another, it constitutes the same offense as the preceding precept.

Except by means of a formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃghakarma), there was a bhikṣu who suffered from consumption; his rag-heap bedding (pāṃsukūla) was so heavy that he was unable to carry it while traveling. The Buddha said:
"He should request three times from the Saṃgha to have a new one made; [the Saṃgha] shall grant it to him by means of a formal motion and announcement (jñaptidvitīya-karman)."
This is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
For a nun, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
The Sangha listens;
when six years have been completed;
or if less than six years have passed, one discards the old [robe] and makes a new one.
If one obtains what has already been completed;
if there is none;
or if another causes it to be made—none of these constitute an offense.
15. The Precept Regarding Not Folding the Sitting Mat.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, he sent someone to invite [the Sangha] for a meal. As was his custom, after the invitation was made, he went to inspect all the rooms.

He saw that the old sitting mats were strewn about everywhere in disorder, with no one to collect them. This was because the bhikṣus, dissatisfied with the thickness, thinness, lightness, or heaviness of their mats, would simply make new ones.
He then established the rule that one should take a piece from an old [sitting mat] to patch a new one.
The group of six monks violated this rule; when the bhikṣus reported their transgression, the Buddha established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must take a piece from an old one measuring one span in length and breadth and patch it onto the new one, for the purpose of destroying its original color."

When he makes a new sitting mat, if the old one has not yet deteriorated and there are no holes in it, he should take it, wash and dye it, stretch it out by pulling, and cut a square piece measuring one span (vitasti) from it. He should then fold this piece and place it upon the new mat—either at the edge or in the center—for the purpose of discoloring it.

If one makes a new sitting mat and does not take a piece of old material, one span in length and breadth, to patch onto the new material for the purpose of discoloration, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether one acts oneself, instructs another, or causes another to act, the offense is established as described above.
For a nun, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
There is no offense in the following cases:
Cut out the old [material] and fold the new over it;
if he has no such material himself, he should have new material made,
or have someone else make it for him.
If it is obtained through exchange, or if it is already pure—there is no offense in either case.
Sixteenth: The precept against carrying wool beyond the limit.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Upananda obtained some sheep’s wool and walked about with it threaded onto the tip of a staff. A householder criticized him, saying, "He is peddling sheep’s wool."
When the monks reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently established a precept:
If a monk, while traveling on a road, obtains wool and there is no one to carry it for him, he may carry it himself for a distance of up to three *yojanas*.
Whether traveling on a journey or staying at a residence, if one obtains wool and has need of it, one may take it; if there is no one to carry it, one may carry it oneself for up to three *yojanas*.
If there is someone present, one should say to them:
"I have this item; help me carry it as far as that place."
"In this interval, a bhikṣu must not assist;
if he does so, it is a duṣkṛta.
If he causes the fourfold assembly of bhikṣuṇīs to carry [the items], and they exceed three yojanas, it is a duṣkṛta."
Except for wool, if one carries other garments such as those made of hemp and so forth, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one carries other items on the end of a staff, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is no one to carry them and one carries them oneself beyond three *yojanas*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture and confession).
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense if she carries it for a distance of three yojanas.
If it is less than three *yojanas*;
if there is a person who speaks for her and does not assist in the interim;
if she sends a nun or any of the fourfold assembly [to speak for her], within the limit of three *yojanas*.
If one carries woolen ornaments or woolen ropes;
or if one carries hair from the head to make a hat or a turban, it is permissible.
17. The precept regarding having a nun who is not a relative wash wool.
The Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu.
The group of six bhikṣus took wool and had nuns wash, dye, and card it.
At that time, the maternal aunt, a nun, had stained her hands with dye while coloring wool; she stood before the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and remained there.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha questioned her, rebuked her, and established a precept.
If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense for the bhikṣu;
it is a duṣkṛta offense for the bhikṣuṇī.
The formation of the offense and its exceptions are as in the "Precept on Washing Old Clothes.
Eighteen: The Precept on Possessing Money and Jewels.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
There was a high minister who, for the sake of Upananda, set aside his portion of food; the son took this food for five coins.
When Upananda arrived, he took the money and deposited it at a market stall.

The laypeople collectively disapproved and the bhikṣus rebuked [the offender]. The King discussed the matter with his ministers, and the Buddha extensively expounded parables; consequently, he rebuked [the offender] and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu, with his own hand, takes hold of money bearing inscriptions or images."
If it be gold or silver, whether one takes hold of it oneself or instructs another to take hold of it, or receives it when placed on the ground, it is a *niḥsargika* offense;

that which must be relinquished therein is as follows: one should speak to the attendant of the monastery who has faith and devotion, or to an upāsaka, saying: "This is not for me to possess; you should know this."
If that person takes it and returns it to the bhikṣu, he should accept it for the sake of that person's property and instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* (a steward) to take charge of it;
if he obtains a pure robe or bowl, he should trade for it and then possess it as his own.
If that upāsaka, having taken [the items], gives them as pure robes and bowls to a bhikṣu, he should accept and take possession of them;
[if he does so], it is a pāyattika.
A bhikṣuṇī commits the same offense.
If one does not say to that person, "Know this; look at this," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if one says, "Know this; look at this," following the aforementioned method of relinquishment (*pratyāśraya*).
If that person is unwilling to give back the robe, the other bhikṣus should say to him:
"The Buddha has given this instruction: 'For the sake of purification, we gave it to you;
you must return this object to its owner.'"
If they still do not give it, [the monk] should go there in person and say:

"The Buddha has instructed that bhikṣus perform the purification ritual and give [the property] to you; you should then bestow it upon the Saṃgha, the stūpa, the upādhyāya, your spiritual friends, and the original donor."
This was because he did not wish to cause the loss of that person's faith-based offerings.
Nineteenth is the precept concerning the trading of money and precious objects.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, Baddhananda went to the marketplace and exchanged money for money.
A layperson criticized and disparaged him, saying, "He is truly skilled at buying and selling.
When the bhikṣus heard this report, the Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.

If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling—whether it be gold already refined, gold not yet refined, or both refined and unrefined gold; silver, which likewise has three types; or coin, which has only one type—and exchanges them with one another.
There are eight kinds of currency: gold, silver, copper, iron, white tin, lead and tin, wooden coins, and foreign resin—these are the eight kinds of money.
[Accepting them constitutes] a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to the offense committed by a bhikṣuṇī.
Other matters concerning the forfeiture of the object, exemptions, and the expedients of seeking precious items are all as in the preceding precept.
There is no offense if one uses money or jewels to trade for necklaces or ornaments, exchanges money for money, or does so for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
20. The Precept Against Trading.
When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time, Upananda went to a village without a permanent residence, exchanged ginger for food, and after eating it, took the remainder with him.
Śāriputra arrived later to beg for alms; when the donor questioned him regarding the matter of Upananda, he was filled with shame and remained silent.
Furthermore, he had gambled for robes with a non-Buddhist, and though he regretted it, he could not recover them.
When the monks reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently established the precept:

"If a bhikṣu exchanges various kinds of *kālika* (timely) medicine for *akālika* (non-timely), *saptāhika* (seven-day), *yāvajjīvika* (lifetime), or *pārihārika* (permissible) medicine—and likewise exchanges them with one another, even exchanging robes for robes."
"Selling" refers to a price of one *kākaṇī* that is repeatedly increased or decreased.
"Increasing the sale" means stating a price of three *kākaṇīs* for something worth one *kākaṇī*.
"Excessively increasing the sale" means stating a price of five *kākaṇīs* for something worth one *kākaṇī*.
Purchasing [the robe] is likewise an offense:
a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. The same offense applies to the bhikṣuṇīs.
There is no offense in the following cases:

the five classes of renunciants may exchange goods among themselves, provided they examine the items carefully for themselves and do not engage in haggling or competitive bargaining as is the custom in the marketplace; furthermore, one must not trade with others who are not members of the Sangha, but must instead have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") conduct the transaction.
If one regrets it, returning is permitted.
If ghee and oil are exchanged for one another, there is no offense.
Twenty-one: The precept against keeping a bowl beyond the limit.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks kept alms bowls; they would discard those that were inferior and constantly sought out fine ones to keep, until their collection became numerous.
When a lay devotee went for a stroll and saw them, he criticized them, saying they were no different from a potter’s shop.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha rebuked them and established this precept:
If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl, there are six kinds:
an iron bowl, a black bowl, a red bowl, a bowl from the country of Suma, a bowl from the country of Ugara, and a bowl from the country of Ujjaya.
There are two main types:
iron bowls and clay bowls.
The large ones hold three *dō* (pecks), and the small ones hold one and a half *dō*; these are the standard measurements for bowls.
It should be held in this manner and should be given as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*).
Regarding the eightfold analysis of the contrast between impure giving and pure giving, it is no different from that in the "Precept on Extra Robes" (*atireka-cīvara-śikṣāpada*).
After ten days had passed, Ānanda obtained a bowl of great value which he wished to offer to Kāśyapa, as it was his own regular use.

Fearing that he would incur the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyantika* since the bowl must be returned within ten days, he informed the Buddha of the matter; the Buddha then relaxed the regulation to allow for a period of ten days.
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The same offense applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*.
The definition of the characteristics and the exceptions are as in the "Excess Garment" (*dīrgha-cīvara*) rule.
22. The Precept Against Seeking Alms Bowls Beyond One’s Entitlement.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Upāli’s brother, Upananda, had his alms bowl broken and sought to possess many additional bowls.
The lay follower calculated the amounts and realized that [the monks] had received much; he then spoke with derision and reproach, saying, "They accept without satiety!
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established a precept.
If a bhikṣu possesses an alms-bowl that has fewer than five mends— each mend being the distance of two finger-widths apart—
and yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, or if it has exactly five mends and is not leaking, yet he seeks a new one, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding "Naiḥsargika" (relinquishment):

having relinquished the bowl within the Saṃgha of this residence, one receives the confession through a single formal motion (*jñapti*). Then, one declares the name of the offense, its category, and its characteristics, and reproves the mind to engender weariness and detachment.
If a bowl is of good quality, it should be confiscated and kept; one should take the lowest-quality, inferior bowl and give it to him.

Then, having performed the formal motion (*jñapti*), one should exchange the bowls in order, starting from the senior monk (*sthavira*): taking the senior monk’s bowl, one gives it to the next seat, and so on, handing them down through the succession until reaching the junior-most monk.
This is a *pāyattika*.
A bhikṣuṇī commits the same offense.
That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it; they shall take the lowest bowl in succession and give it to him to keep until it breaks, at which point he should continue to keep it.
This is the proper time.
The Saṃgha shall give [the bowl] by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

The recipient should guard it. One must not place it where tiles or stones might fall, nor beneath a staff or a sword, nor beneath a suspended object, nor on a path, nor upon a stone, nor beneath a fruit tree, nor on uneven ground. One must not place it inside a window, nor beneath a door-panel, nor under a bed or in a corner of a bed, except for temporary placement.
One must not place it between two beds, nor stand and shake the bowl until it is broken by one's feet.
If one intentionally damages it, loses it, or uses it for purposes other than those for which a bowl is intended, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
if the robe has five patches or fewer; if one seeks a new one because the existing one is worn out;
or if one requests it from a relative.
If one solicits from a renunciant;
or if it is for another; or if another acts on one's behalf.
If one obtains it without seeking;
or if one obtains it after having given [something in exchange];
or if one purchases livestock with one's own funds—none of these constitute an offense.
23. The Precept Against Begging for Thread and Having a Non-Relative Weaver Weave It.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

While Upāli (Bhadanta) was sewing a saṃghāṭī robe, he begged for thread until it became excessive; he then took the thread and had a weaver weave it, personally winding the spools and supervising the weaving.
Householders criticized and disparaged them, and the bhikṣus reported these transgressions.
The Buddha then rebuked them and established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu begs for thread himself, he may beg for it from various places."
"Thread" refers to the ten kinds of cloth thread.
If one causes a weaver who is not a relative to weave a robe, there is no offense provided that both the weaver and the provider of the thread are relatives.
To give thread to one who is not a relative is a *duṣkṛta*.
To watch someone weave, to weave for oneself, or to spin thread is also a *duṣkṛta*.
[If the cloth is completed, it is] a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The same applies to the offense for a bhikṣuṇī.
There is no offense in the following cases: if both are relatives;

If one weaves for oneself a bowl bag, a leather sandal bag, a needle-cushion, a meditation belt, a waistband, a cap, socks, a heat-retaining cloth, or a cloth for wrapping leather sandals, it is permissible.
24. The Precept on Exhorting the Weaver to Increase the Thread.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A householder provided thread to a weaver to make a robe for Upananda; later, when he arrived home, he selected the finest thread and gave it to the weaver to weave, and further promised him payment.
The laypeople criticized and disparaged them, and the bhikṣus reported their transgression.
The Buddha, because of this, rebuked them and established a rule:

"If a householder or a householder’s wife employs a weaver to weave a robe for a bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu has not previously received an invitation of his own accord, if the householder gives the bhikṣu a robe of high value, he is permitted—provided he is one who is content with few desires—to request one that is inferior, according to his wish."
He then went to the weaver’s place and said to him, “This robe is being made for me;
weave it for me with the utmost care, making it wide, large, firm, and fine. I shall give you a certain amount as payment.”
If that bhikṣu gives the price—even as much as the value of a single meal—and obtains a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he seeks a robe but does not obtain one, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies to nuns regarding this offense.
There is no offense in cases where one seeks less than what was requested, or seeks from a relative, or seeks from a renunciant, or when another person acts on one's behalf.
Twenty-five: The precept against taking a bhikṣu’s robe.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Nanda’s disciple was skilled at exhortation and conversion.
Upananda wished to travel together with him, so he first gave him a robe.
The other bhikṣus said, "He is ignorant;
he does not know how to recite the precepts, proclaim the precepts, perform the poṣadha, or carry out formal acts (karmavācanā).
Later, when they departed and did not follow him, he immediately seized their robes.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who consequently established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger, either seizes it himself or instructs another to seize it, saying, 'Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you';
if, out of anger, he seizes it himself or instructs another to seize it and then conceals it, he commits an offense."
If one takes [an object] that has not yet been stored away, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is placed upon a tree, a shelf, a bed, or any other location, and one moves it from that place, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one takes it without moving it from its place, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If she returns the robe or takes it back, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Nuns commit this offense in the same manner as monks. There is no offense in the following cases:
If one does not feel anger and says, "I regret it; I will not give it to you, so return my robe to me," and the other person knows that he regrets it, the robe may be returned immediately;
or if another person says, "This bhikṣu wishes to regret it," the robe should be returned to him.
If one borrows another's robe and wears it improperly, and the owner takes it back, there is no offense.

If one fears it will be lost or damaged, or if that person has broken their precepts, broken their views, or broken their deportment; or if they have been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), have been expelled (*pabbājanīya-kamma*), or are deserving of expulsion; or if, for the sake of this matter, there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacariya-pariyāya*)—if one takes back all such items without concealing or storing them away, in all these cases there is no offense.
26. The precept against keeping seven-day medicine beyond the limit.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
During the autumn months, a monk’s wind-disorder (vāta-roga) was aggravated; his body became emaciated and sores broke out. The Buddha said:
"There are ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and fat; it is permitted to consume them at the proper or improper times when there is a cause for illness.
While the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, the community of Pilindavatsa accumulated and hoarded vast quantities of goods.
The monastics and laypeople censured this, and they reported it to the Buddha,
who rebuked him and established a regulation: "If a bhikṣu is ill and a physician instructs him to take a certain kind of medicine,
he may consume the remaining ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar for up to seven days."
The meaning of the eight categories of phrases is as previously explained in the "Robe Precept.

If one consumes [the medicine] beyond seven days, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; having relinquished it to the Saṃgha, and after the formal confession of the offense has been completed, the procedure for returning that medicine is as follows:
on the seventh day, one relinquishes it to a bhikṣu, who should then take and consume it.
If seven days have passed, one should smear butter and oil on the door and threshold, and give honey and rock sugar to the park keeper;
if less than seven days have passed, one should return it by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the bhikṣus should take it for smearing their feet or lighting lamps.
This is a *pāyattika*.
The same offense applies to a bhikṣuṇī.
There is no offense in cases where there are distinctions such as those mentioned above regarding relinquishing or using [the object].
27. The Precept Regarding Seeking Rain-Clothing Before the Proper Time and Using It Before the Proper Time.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The mother of Viśākhā invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
When the maidservant announced that it was time for the meal, she saw the bhikṣus bathing naked.
She consequently made eight vows, which were praised by the Buddha.
The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) constantly sought out [faults], and the bhikṣus reported their transgressions.
The Buddha, because of this, established a precept:
"If a month remains of the spring season, a bhikṣu should seek a rain-bathing robe. A 'rain-bathing robe' is one that a bhikṣu uses for bathing in the rain."
There are ten kinds of robes;
one should seek them on the sixteenth day of the third month,
and they should be used for bathing during the half-month.
It should be used starting from the first day of the fourth month.
If a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bath robe more than one month in advance, or seeks a rainy-season robe before the sixteenth day of the third month, [he commits an offense].
To use it for bathing more than half a month prior— meaning before the first day of the fourth month—
is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣu and a *duṣkṛta* offense for a bhikṣuṇī.
There is no offense if one abandons it for another use, or if one wears it while bathing, or washes it, or puts it away; these are not offenses.
Twenty-eight: The precept against receiving urgent offerings of robes before the prescribed time and keeping them after the prescribed time has passed.
When the Buddha was at Pārileyyaka, he permitted the acceptance of summer robes.
The group of six monks constantly begged for robes and constantly accepted robes.
Upananda entered the rains retreat in one place and accepted his robes in another.
While the Buddha was observing the summer retreat at Śrāvastī, a high minister made offerings for the retreat; the Buddha, on that account, relaxed the rule and then established it as a precept:
"If a bhikṣu, during the final ten days of the three-month summer retreat—meaning from the seventh day of the seventh month onwards until the fifteenth day—is [in such a situation...]"
When the bhikṣus receive robes offered during a time of urgency, they obtain them if they accept them, but lose them if they do not; therefore, it is called "urgent.
There are ten kinds of such robes.
A bhikṣu who knows this to be an urgent gift of robes should accept it;
having accepted it, he may keep it until the time for robes.
The "time for robes" is one month after the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, or five months if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread.
If ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and one obtains an urgently offered robe (*ātyayika-cīvara*), having accepted it, one may store it for one month or five months.
Even if it must be accepted tomorrow before the *pravāraṇā*, the period of storage is increased by nine days beyond the one-month or five-month limit.
If one keeps it beyond that limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This refers to an "urgent gift of robes" (*ātyayikacīvara*); if one keeps it before the prescribed time or after the prescribed time, one commits an offense of falling (*pāyattika*).
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
There is no offense if one does not go before [the time] nor after [the time]. There is no offense.
If robes have been taken away or lost, and one takes them back after the [prescribed] time, there is no offense.
If a monk who has entrusted his robes travels far away and the water or land routes are cut off, it is no offense even if he goes beyond the [prescribed] time.
29. The precept concerning the offense of exceeding the limit of separation from one's robes while staying in the wilderness (*araṇya*).

When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu dwelling in the wilderness was beaten by bandits and his belongings were plundered. The Buddha then commanded that each individual robe be left inside a village dwelling.
The group of six monks traveled while entrusting their robes to others.
Their companions reported this transgression, and the Buddha, being weary, established a restrictive rule:
"If a bhikṣu, at the conclusion of the three months of the summer retreat, after the completion of the month of Kārttika—that is, after the middle of the eighth month—"
In an araṇya, one should be five hundred bows' distance from a village. In the country of Cāmara, a bow is four cubits long; this measurement refers to the "middle" cubit (*madhyama-hasta*).
If there is doubt, or if there is suspicion of bandits and thieves, [one should remain at that distance].
In a place of fear, there are terrifying thieves and robbers.
A bhikṣu dwelling in such a place may wish to leave one of his three robes inside a village dwelling; here, "village" means a settlement.
If monks have a legitimate reason to stay apart from their robes for up to six nights,

and they continue to stay apart from their robes due to that reason, then on the seventh night, before the first light of dawn has appeared, they must either relinquish [the robe], take hold of the robe, or reach a place where a stone can be thrown.
The opposite of the above constitutes an offense.
If it exceeds [the permitted duration], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The exceptions are as previously stated in the "Rule on Being Separated from One’s Robe."
30. The Precept on Diverting Property Belonging to the Sangha.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A householder provided a meal for the Saṃgha and offered robes as a gift; when Bāḍhananda heard of this, he said to him:
"There are many who give to the Saṃgha; you should now give to me.
Later, when the householder saw that the elder bhikṣu was fully endowed with dignified deportment, he immediately felt regret and sighed in admiration.
When a bhikṣu pointed out a transgression, the Buddha consequently established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu, whether knowing or not knowing, [acts in such a way], there is no offense.
Regarding monastic property (saṃghika-vastu), there are three kinds:
"Property belonging to the Saṃgha" refers to that which has already been assigned to the Saṃgha;
"for the sake of the Saṃgha" refers to that which is being made for the Saṃgha but has not yet been assigned to the Saṃgha;
"already given to the Saṃgha" refers to that which has already been assigned to the Saṃgha and has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha.
"Objects" refers to items down to drinking vessels.
As for those things one seeks to take into one's own possession: if they were intended for the Sangha, one transfers them to the Stūpa;
if they were intended for the Sangha of the four quarters, one transfers them to the present Sangha.
Whether it be a monk or a nun;
whether it be at different locations;
or if the aforementioned cases are reversed or interchanged;
If one has doubt or a mistaken perception— both constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
[In the case of a formal] *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, there is no offense in the following circumstances:
If one does not know;
if one has the perception that it is not permitted;
or if one permits only a small amount but encourages [the donor] to give more.
If one gives to few people while encouraging others to give to many;
or encourages them to give excellent things;
or speaks jokingly;
If one speaks erroneously— there is no offense in either case. Venerable sirs,
I have finished reciting the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
(This is asked) three times.
Venerable sirs!
Since you are silent, you are pure in this matter.
Thus shall this matter be upheld.

Come. First, the precept against intentional lying.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
The Śākya son Hastibala was skilled in debate; when he engaged in discussion with non-Buddhists and found himself at a disadvantage, he would reverse his previous statements;
likewise, when questioned within the Saṃgha, he would again contradict his words.
A brahmin criticized [the monks] for lacking the True Dharma, and a bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha.
Consequently, this precept was established:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing—whether by seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing, as well as not seeing, not hearing, not sensing, or not cognizing—[makes such a claim], there are eight types [of cases]."
As for "that which sees," it is the visual consciousness that sees,
up to and including the mental consciousness that cognizes.
As for "that which does not see," this refers to the remaining five consciousnesses, excluding the visual consciousness.
The same applies to the opposite cases.

Furthermore, regarding one who speaks falsely: if the object is something seen, heard, touched, or known, or if it is a mere thought, or a doubt, yet they say they have not seen, heard, touched, or known it, it is a *pāyattika*.
This applies similarly even to cases of not seeing, hearing, and so forth.
If one originally forms the intention to speak falsely but does not recall it as a false statement at the time of speaking, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing);
if one does not recall it before or after, but knows it is a false statement while actually speaking it, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

If what one sees is different, what one endures is different, what one desires is different, what one contacts is different, what one perceives is different, and what one thinks is different—such matters as these are all false speech.
When the *poṣadha* is being recited, if one remembers an offense but does not confess it even after the question has been asked three times, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
[if one fails to confess after the third questioning], it is a *pāyattika*. If the recitation is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the *bhikṣuṇī* commits the same offense, the three other assemblies commit a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the eight cases, such as saying "I did not see" when one has not seen, up to saying "I know" when one knows, and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no offense if one speaks according to what one perceives in one's mind.
2. The precept against verbal abuse.

While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks engaged in abusive speech based on personal origins before those presiding over legal cases. The latter became confused and lost track of the proceedings; feeling ashamed, they remained silent.
The bhikṣu reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha then drew upon the analogy of a bull, saying, "An animal may be ruined and is incapable of advancing with strength," and so forth, before enacting this precept.

If a monk, regarding one of various types—born into a low-caste family, of lowly occupation, or of lowly skills and crafts—should say to him: "You have committed an offense," or "You are full of fetters and defilements," or use such words as "blind" or "one-eyed."

Regarding disparaging speech: if one reviles another bhikṣu in any of the six ways mentioned above—whether by direct insult, by metaphorical insult, or by comparing oneself to them—one commits a pāyattika;
if the speech is incoherent or incomplete, it is a duṣkṛta.
It is a *pāyattika*.
If one reviles another by speaking of their virtuous qualities, saying, "You are an *araṇya* [forest-dweller]," or even "You are a practitioner of meditation";
or if one reviles them by way of comparison, saying, "You resemble a practitioner of meditation."
If one reviles oneself by saying, "I am not [a monk]," whether the statement is completed or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the other three groups of disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense in cases where one speaks for the sake of mutual benefit; for the sake of the Dharma, the Vinaya, or instruction; out of affection; or when speaking in jest, by inadvertence, or through error.
3. The precept against divisive speech.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks spread rumors back and forth among others, causing the community to fall into strife that they were unable to quell.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
He then cited the example: "If a jackal can cause strife between two beasts, how much more so among humans? Having thus rebuked them, he established this precept.
If a bhikṣu speaks with double-tongued speech— meaning he speaks to cause strife among a group of ten, desiring to separate those on this side from those on that side—
it is a pāyattika.
There is no offense if it is for the purpose of breaking up evil associates or evil factions.

If one’s preceptor, fellow teacher, spiritual friend, relative, or frequent interlocutor speaks repeatedly what is meaningless and unbeneficial, and if one wishes to employ skillful means to bring about what is beneficial and to correct such a person, there is no offense.
4. The precept against staying overnight with a woman.

While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, Aniruddha went to stay overnight at the house of a courtesan. When the woman came toward him naked to disturb him, the Venerable One ascended into the air. She felt shame and repented; he preached the Dharma for her, and she attained the Path.
When a bhikṣu was accused of an offense, the Buddha then rebuked him and established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu, with a woman who is a human female and possesses discernment, and whose life-faculty is not severed..."
A "room" (śālā) has walls on all four sides and a roof above;
alternatively, it may be open at the front and lack walls;
or, although it has a roof, it is not complete.
Or it may be covered entirely except for an opening. Regarding "lying down":

whether one arrives before or after [the time], or arrives simultaneously; whether one is reclining or fully prostrate; whichever side of the body touches the ground, or whichever way one turns over—each constitutes an offense.
It is a *pāyattika*.
If one sleeps together with a non-human female, a female animal, a eunuch, or a person with dual sexual organs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
During the daytime, if a woman stands while a bhikṣu lies down, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one does not know that there is a woman inside the room;
or if the room is uncovered; or if it is half-enclosed, partially enclosed, or fully enclosed.
If it is half-covered or obstructed, the formulation of the sentence follows the same principle as above;
likewise if one is lying ill or bound.
Regarding the precepts on [the dangers of] life and Brahmā, etc.—these are all opened up.
Fifth, the precept concerning the offense of staying overnight with one who has not received full ordination beyond the limit.
The Buddha was at the city of Kalandaka.
The group of six monks stayed together in an elder’s lecture hall; at that time, they fell asleep with distracted minds and their bodies were exposed, leading to mockery by others.
They informed the Buddha, who consequently established this precept.
While the Buddha was in Kauśāmbī, he permitted staying for two or three nights, and thus this rule was again formulated as a formal precept.
If a bhikṣu stays overnight— meaning he shares a room— with a person who has not received the full ordination (excluding bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs), that is,
with any other such person who has not received the full ordination, it is as previously described.
If two nights have passed and one reaches the third night—whether staying for two nights or three—if the dawn has not yet appeared, one should rise and depart.
Upon reaching the fourth night, one should either leave oneself or send someone who has not yet received the precepts to leave.
It is a *pāyattika*.
If one stays together with a non-human or a male animal for more than three nights, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta*.
The exceptions are the same as those in the preceding precept.
Sixth, reciting the precepts together with those who have not yet received full ordination.

When the Buddha was staying at the city of Khāṇumata, the group of six bhikṣus were reciting sūtras in the lecture hall with various elders; their voices were so loud that they disturbed those engaged in meditation.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept:
If a bhikṣu recites together with a person who has not received the full ordination as described above—
meaning they recite together the meaning of the phrases, the meaning of the syllables, and the meaning of the characters.
The same applies to "non-sentential meaning" (*apada-artha*).
"Sentential meaning" refers to reciting together without one preceding or following the other.
"Non-sentential meaning" is, for example, when one person has not yet finished saying "Commit no evil," and another person repeats it immediately.
Regarding "phrases and meanings," this refers to [statements] such as "the eye is impermanent.
Regarding "non-phrases and non-meanings," this refers to excerpts from the preceding [text].
Regarding "the meaning of syllables," this refers to reciting the syllable "A" together.
"Non-literal meaning" refers to the preceding syllable "A.
"Dharma" refers to the True Dharma spoken by Buddhas, śrāvakas, sages, and devas.
It is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one recites together [with another], whether saying it once, twice, or thrice; or if teaching by word of mouth or by writing; or if the words are not clearly articulated;
or if the recipient is a non-human or an animal—in all these cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the teacher does not instruct, saying, "When I have finished speaking, you may speak," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for the teacher.
There is no offense if [the teacher says], "When I have finished speaking, you speak."
When one person has finished reciting, another writes it down;
or if those with the same practice recite together.
Should there be joking speech, talking to oneself, or mistakenly speaking of this or that [person], none of these constitute an offense.
7. The Precept on Proclaiming Gross Offenses.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

There were certain *parivāsa* and *mānatva* monks who were seated in the lower rank; the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) then disclosed their transgressions to laypeople. Those who had committed offenses, as well as the other monks, were all filled with shame.
The Buddha censured and prohibited [the act] because a bhikṣu had raised a charge against another.
If a bhikṣu knows that the other person is innocent, he is permitted [to raise the charge].
There are grave offenses: the four pārājikas and the saṃghāvaśeṣas.
To speak to one who has not yet received the full ordination (upasampadā), except by formal monastic authorization (saṃgha-kamma), constitutes a pāyattika offense.
To speak of a minor offense when it is actually a grave offense (sthūlātyaya),
or to speak of one's own grave offense or another person’s offense [when it is a minor one], constitutes a dukkaṭa offense in all such cases.
There is no offense if one does not know; or if the assembly has previously appointed [the person]; or if there was no perception of coarseness; or if a layperson had already heard it before. Eighth:
To falsely claim to have attained the Path and speak of the precepts to a layperson.
While the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, after having assembled the Saṃgha and rebuked him on account of his previous "great lie," he then established this precept:
If a bhikṣu speaks of a superhuman state (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) to a person who has not received full ordination, saying, "I have seen this; I have known this," and it is true, it is a *pāyattika*.
This is also as in the first section above.
If it was said to be karmic retribution, or if it was done in jest or by mistake, there is no offense.
Ninth: The precept against preaching the Dharma alone to a woman.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

Kālodāyin was whispering the Dharma to his daughter-in-law in front of her mother-in-law. Because of his mother-in-law’s reproachful questioning, the monks reported his transgression, and the Buddha consequently established a prohibition against it.
Later, [the rule was expanded to include] speaking more than five or six words, or explaining [the Dharma] beyond the limit to a man who possesses discernment.
If a bhikṣu, as described above, speaks the Dharma to a woman, exceeding [five words], such as:
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without self."
There are six statements: that the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent;
and, excluding a man of wisdom, [the statement regarding] matters that are coarse and evil or not coarse and evil.
It is a *pāyattika*.
If one speaks and it is not understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if one speaks toward a non-human or an animal, the offense is likewise.
There is no offense if:
it consists of five or six words;
or if it is spoken in the presence of an intelligent man.
If there is no wise man present to ask questions, one should answer by explaining in detail;
if conferring the five precepts upon a female lay follower (upāsikā), one should explain the dharma of the five precepts up to that point;
if bestowing the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), one should explain the dharma of the eightfold fast, the eightfold noble path, and the ten unwholesome dharmas.
When a woman asks about the meaning [of the Dharma] and does not understand, it is permissible to explain it extensively.
Tenth, the precept against digging the earth.
The Buddha was staying at the city of Kalandaka.

The group of six monks were repairing a lecture hall for the Buddha; they dug the ground all around it themselves, leading a householder to criticize and disparage them, saying, "They do not understand the True Dharma, for they have severed the life-roots of others."
He informed the Buddha, who thereupon established a rule.
Later, while instructing others on how to repair the lecture hall, he said, "Dig here; place it there.
The elder rebuked him severely, and the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, who again established a precept.

If a bhikṣu digs with his own hand, or uses a hoe, a mattock, or a mallet to strike, or even pinches and scratches with his fingernails, or drives a stake into the ground, or kindles a fire upon the ground, and has the perception that it is ground.
Regarding the earth: if it has not been dug;
or if the earth has already been dug but has been soaked by rain for four months and has returned to its original state.
If one instructs another to dig, and does not instruct them by saying, "Look at this" or "Know this," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
A *pāyattika* offense.
For the two lower assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*; the same applies to the subsequent sections.
There is no offense if one says, "I know this; look at this."

If one drags timber, supports a fence to straighten it, turns over bricks or stones, takes cow dung, or takes earth from a collapsed bank or rat-infested soil—excluding earth from walking paths and earth within a dwelling—if one comes and goes on a walking path or sweeps the ground without intentionally digging, there is no offense in any of these cases.
11. The precept against destroying the seeds of living beings.
While the Buddha was at the City of Wilds (Kalandaka), he assembled the Saṃgha and declared:
"There was a bhikṣu who, while repairing a dwelling, cut down a tree himself; this is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa."
This is a precept established through censure.
If a bhikṣu damages, cuts, hacks, or causes to fall, it is all termed "damaging.
This refers to non-human beings such as ghosts and spirits.
A village consists of all grasses and trees, which are the dwelling places of ghosts and animals.
There are five kinds of villages:
those propagated from roots, those propagated from branches, those propagated from joints, those propagated from bulbous roots, and those propagated from seeds.
It is a *pāyattika*.
If one perceives it as living and cuts it oneself, instructs another to cut it, roasts it oneself, or cooks it—whether doing so personally or instructing another—one falls [into an offense].
If one acts while harboring doubt, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the seven types of colors found in plants and trees, if one destroys them oneself or instructs another to destroy them, one falls into an offense.
If one harbors doubt or forms the intention [to destroy them], it is a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅).
If one drives a stake into living grass or trees, or uses fire and the like against them, one likewise falls into an offense.
If one cuts down a majority of growing grass or trees, one falls [into an offense].
If one cuts half-dry or half-living [grass or trees], or if one does not say, "I know this" or "I see this," it is all a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).
There is no offense if one says,
"Look at this; know this," or if one cuts dry and withered grass or wood.
If one drags timber or bamboo across living grass or plants, erects a fence or screen, moves stones from a moat, or collects cow dung;
or if one uses a staff to clear away living grass covering a path;
or if one props up something with tiles or stones and thereby damages or cuts the grass and plants.
If one removes the soil from a walking path, sweeps the walking path, or strikes the ground with a staff, and by mistake knocks over or cuts living grass, there is no offense.
12. The Precept on Annoying Others with Evasive Speech.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
The bhikṣu Chanda committed an offense; when other bhikṣus questioned him about it, he answered with irrelevant matters.
He reported the matter to the Buddha; after the Buddha had rebuked him, he made a report using evasive speech.
Subsequently, he caused trouble for the Saṃgha: when summoned, he would not come, and so on, up to speaking when he should not speak.
He reported this matter to the Buddha. After the Buddha had rebuked him, he made a report that was intended to cause provocation;
it was on account of this that the rule was established. "If a bhikṣu falsely makes evasive speech before the Saṃgha has been informed—'To whom were you speaking?'"
"What did he speak about? What principle did he discuss?
Did he speak for my sake, or for the sake of others?"
Regarding the phrase "I do not see this offense," it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in all cases.
If one speaks thus after the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
Regarding "disturbing others," as in the preceding context, even down to speaking when one should not speak, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
Once the announcement has been made, if the one who is to act does not do so, it is a *pāyattika*.
It is a *pāyattika*.
If the senior monk calls and [the junior] does not come, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is deaf and does not understand; if there were errors or omissions in the preceding speech; if one asks, "To whom did you speak? up to "I do not see this offense";
or if a *karmavācanā* (formal act) is performed that is illegal or without benefit, and one does not join in it, or is summoned but does not come.
If an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act) is being performed, and one does not wish to know of it, yet is told "Do not come" and nevertheless comes;
or if one eats in a single sitting, or eats without performing the *kṛtāvadāna* (the ritual of leaving food), or is ill, and is called to rise but does not rise;
or during life-threatening or *brahman*-related calamities, one is told "Do not rise" and nevertheless rises; [in all such cases, there is no offense].
If one asks with an evil mind, do not speak to them;
if they commit an unrighteous act, then reprimand them;
or if they speak in a low voice.
If one speaks erroneously—there is no offense in any case.
Thirteen: The precept against disparaging or reviling the administrators.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
The bhikṣu Trapusa was appointed by the Saṃgha to oversee its affairs; the bhikṣu Mālukyaputra, from a place within range of his vision, criticized him with disdain.
When this transgression was reported to the Buddha, he rebuked him and established a precept.
Subsequently, he reviled [the monk] in a place where he could hear him; because the offense was grave, he informed the Buddha, who then established a further regulation based on the previous one.
If a bhikṣu, out of malice—meaning while face-to-face but not within earshot—says, "He is possessed of attachment, hatred, fear, or delusion."
To revile means to hear [the words] from behind one's back and to utter insults where one cannot see the person.
This is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not accept the instruction of the elder and instead harbors resentment and reviles him, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
if there is a factual basis for the matter and, fearing future regret, one says "there is attachment" and so forth in order to prompt the other person to confess according to the Dharma;
or if it was said in jest or by mistake—none of these constitute an offense.
14. The Precept Regarding Spreading the Community’s Property on Open Ground.

When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, an elder invited the Saṃgha. The group of seventeen bhikṣus took the community’s sitting mats and spread them out on the open ground for walking meditation. Expecting that mealtime would arrive, they did not fold them up and went to eat. Consequently, they were covered by wind-blown dust and soil, and ruined and defiled by insects and birds.
Having reported this transgression to the Buddha, the Buddha rebuked him and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu takes property belonging to the Saṃgha—there are three types: for the Saṃgha, from the Saṃgha, or belonging to the Saṃgha—[such as] a rope bed, of which there are five kinds:"
Regarding the *khuñja-pāda*, *ṛju-pāda*, *vakra-pāda*, *śalākā-praveśa*, and legless wooden beds, they are also as described above.
As for bedding, it may be used either for sitting or for lying down.
Regarding sitting mats intended for regular use:
if one spreads them on an open ground, or instructs another to spread them, and then departs without personally putting them away or instructing another to put them away, it is a *pāyattika*.
He hands over the property of the Saṃgha to the administrator, saying:
"I now entrust this to you; guard and look after it.
If there is no one at all, he should deposit it in a secluded place.
If there is no place of concealment, and one knows for certain that there will be no damage, one should take the coarse cloth and cover it over the fine cloth.
If one intends to return immediately, one should depart.
One should go if one can return as quickly as the rain falls.
If he proceeds by employing such means as these, he should depart;
if he does not do so, he falls [into an offense] upon first stepping out the door.
If he employs the means but then regrets it and turns back, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If two persons are sitting together, the one of lower rank should collect [the bedding]; if he does not, he commits two offenses, while the one of higher rank commits one *pāyattika* offense.
If neither collects it, both commit a *pāyattika* offense.
If one fails to put away other beds, stools, machines, and so forth, as well as the outer and inner linings of bedding, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one spreads out monastic property in the open and enters a room to meditate, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if monastic property is laid out in the open, and upon departing, one informs those who have resided there previously, the *māmāṭi*, or the administrator; or if one employs the aforementioned expedient means—in all such instances, there is no offense.
15. The Precept on Covering and Spreading Monastic Property.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A visiting bhikṣu spread out bedding in a peripheral room to sleep; without informing anyone, he departed. Consequently, the bedding became moldy and ruined, infested by insects, and its color faded.
Having witnessed this, he informed the Buddha, who consequently established this precept:

"If a bhikṣu, having spread out communal bedding in a monastic dwelling—such as rope beds, wooden beds, mattresses, sitting mats, pillows, floor coverings, down to mere woolen blankets—[and departs without restoring them, it is an offense]."

If one spreads out [a seat] oneself or instructs another to spread it, and then sits or lies down upon it, yet upon departing neither raises it oneself nor instructs another to raise it, one should say to the resident bhikṣu:
"Please secure it well for me."

If there is no one present and he does not fear losing anything, he should move the bed away from the wall, prop up the legs of the bed high, place his pillow, mattress, and bedding inside it, and cover them over with other coarse materials;
or, fearing they might be damaged, he should take the bedding and other items and place them on a clothing rack, then stand the bed upright and depart.
If one does not do so and goes beyond the boundary, one commits a *pāyattika* offense;
