if one intends to leave but regrets it and returns, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one returns immediately and does not stay long, it is permitted to remain outside the boundary for two nights.
If, during the third watch before the appearance of dawn, one does not go oneself nor dispatch a messenger to protect [the robe], it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
Regarding non-offenses:

as described above, if after having made the necessary preparations, one is outside the boundary where the paths by water or land are cut off due to circumstances such as threats to life or the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya), it is permitted.
16. The Precept on Forcibly Spreading Out a Seat.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

The group of six and the group of seventeen were traveling along the same road and arrived at a place where no one lived. The group of seventeen sought lodging for themselves; knowing that they had found a place to stay, the group of six forcibly spread out bedding in the middle of it and stayed there.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu, whether he knows it or not,
enters a dwelling where another bhikṣu is already staying, and later forcibly takes up residence in the middle, at the head, at the feet, or at either side."
If one spreads bedding— whether grass mats, leaf mats, or down to mere ground coverings or woolen rugs—

and stays overnight with the thought, "If they find it cramped, they will naturally move away from me," doing so for this specific reason and no other, and failing to maintain proper decorum, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
This refers to turning over onto one's side with the ribs touching the bed, resulting in a formal offense (pārājika).
There is no offense if one was unaware beforehand.
If one has already spoken and [the space] remains occupied, one should first ask for leave;
if the space is wide and spacious, such that there is no obstruction or hindrance;
or if an acquaintance says, "Just spread it out, I myself shall speak to the host"; [in these cases, one may proceed].
If one falls to the ground;
if one is ill and rolls over, thereby falling upon it;
or if one is held by force.
If one is imprisoned;
or if there are the two difficulties of life or the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya)—in these cases, there is no offense.
Seventeen: The precept against forcibly ejecting another from a room.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six and the group of seventeen were traveling along the same road and arrived at a small dwelling place.
The group of seventeen entered the monastery first and swept and sprinkled it until it was clean.
The group of six monks, knowing of a desirable location, drove [a monk] out and pulled him away.
The bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who then established this precept:

If a bhikṣu, being angry with another bhikṣu and displeased with him, within a monastic dwelling, either pulls him out himself or instructs another to pull him out; whether he acts himself or instructs others to pull him out, for every person pulled out and for every room they exit, a transgression is committed accordingly.
If one leads many people out through a single door, or leads a single person out through many doors, in all such cases one commits multiple *pāyattika* offenses.
If one person exits through a single door, it is one *pāyattika* offense.
If one carries out another's belongings, or throws them outside the door, or closes the door on another's belongings, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense;
[if committed intentionally], it is a *pāyattika*. There is no offense in the following cases:
One who is free from ill will may leave in due order; likewise,
one who has been sent away before receiving full ordination,
or one who has violated the precepts, views, or deportment, or who has been subject to formal censure or suspension.
For this reason, those whom the Māra Pāpīyān and Brahmā Sahāmpati attempted to drive out were all released.
Eighteen: The precept against sitting on a bed with detachable legs.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A bhikṣu was staying on an upper story of a multi-storied building. He sat upon a stool with detachable legs, and the leg detached and fell onto the bhikṣu.
His body was injured and he bled; looking upward, he cursed in anger.
When the monks reported this transgression, the Buddha rebuked them and established a rule:
"If a bhikṣu, whether in a communal dwelling (saṃghārāma) or a private dwelling,
stands upon an upper story such that his head does not reach the ceiling."
Regarding a rope bed with removable legs or a wooden bed with removable legs: "removable legs" refers to legs that are inserted into sockets.
Whether sitting or lying down, one should ensure that the side of the body rests against the bed as one turns over.
A *pāyattika* offense.
With the exception of a bed with detachable legs, if one sits on a single-seated chair, a plank bed, or a layperson’s bed, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
If one sits on a bed with swiveling legs, straight legs, curved legs, or no legs;
if the supports of the bed are too large;
or if the legs of a removable-bed frame are fitted with narrow tenons; [these are all improper].
If it is a multi-storied building with a wooden plank roof, or one covered with carved woodwork resembling flowers, or one with a thick covering;
or if it is a plank bed;
or if one sits on a bed with removable legs—all these are permitted.
19. The Precept Regarding Water Containing Insects.
The Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī.
Chanda was building a house and used water containing insects to mix with the mud; he instructed his laborers to do so. A householder saw this and felt resentment.
“There is no true Dharma in taking the lives of sentient beings!
Thus did the bhikṣu point out the transgression, and the Buddha, on that account, established the precept:
“If a bhikṣu [acts], whether he knows it or not, there is no offense.”

If there are insects in water, whether one pours it onto mud or grass, or instructs another to pour it; or if one throws grass or soil into the water where the insects are; or if one pours fermented milk, clear fermented milk, or vinegar onto mud or grass—any such act constitutes an offense.
The same applies to instructing others;
it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
If one does not know there are insects but perceives them as being none,
or if the insects are large, one may move the water with the hand to make them leave;
or one may strain the water and sprinkle it upon the ground.
If one instructs another to strain [the water], there is no offense in any case.
Twenty: The precept against exceeding the limit when roofing a house.
The Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī.
Chanda built a room and continued to add layers of roofing without ceasing; the roof then collapsed and broke. A lay devotee remarked with disapproval:
"Though the donor may give, the recipient should know contentment."
When the monks reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently established the precept:
"If a monk constructs a large dwelling and expends much wealth and property on it—
engraving, carving, painting, or decorating the doors, windows, and other embellishments."
Regarding the instruction for covering with thatch, there are two types: covering lengthwise and covering crosswise.
It should be level with two or three joints.
If it exceeds this, while the bhikṣu is still instructing on the third joint and it has not yet been finished, he must go to a place where he is neither seen nor heard.
If one does not go to a place where [the matter] can be seen or heard, and the three intervals are completed,
it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one alternately abandons the places where [the matter] can be seen or heard, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in cases such as those previously specified where one has been instructed or where the person is at a great distance.
Twenty-one: Teaching the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts arbitrarily.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

When the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī came to request instruction, the Buddha ordered that someone from the Saṃgha be sent; it was Paṇḍaka’s turn to go there and preach the Dharma. When it was the turn of the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks to go, they instead spoke of worldly discourse.
Āṭavikā informed the Buddha, who then performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to appoint her and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha performs a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a single formal act (*karma*),
neither appoints another nor makes a formal motion (*jñapti*) within the Saṃgha [to do so], [he commits an offense]."
The eight rules that must not be transgressed are fully set forth in the *Vinaya*.
For a bhikṣuṇī [to fail to observe these], it is a pāyattika offense.

If, at the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), after the questions and answers on the seat have been concluded, a bhikṣu has been appointed by the Saṃgha or invited by the bhikṣuṇīs; he arrives at the appointed time, and the bhikṣuṇīs likewise meet him at the appointed time.
If one violates this, both commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one hears that [a guest] is coming, one should go out half a *yojana* to welcome them and provide whatever they require; failure to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Sangha has not appointed him and it is not the day for instruction, yet he explains the eight rules that must not be violated, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if he explains the Dharma when he has not been appointed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the Sangha is ill, discordant, or incomplete, one should send someone to pay homage and inquire after their health;
likewise, if the community of nuns is ill and so forth, one should also send someone to pay homage and inquire after their health—if this is not done, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For the two assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

There is no offense if, after the bhikṣuṇī assembly has performed the aforementioned preparatory rites, the paths by water or land are cut off or other obstacles arise such that they cannot be accommodated for prostrating and inquiring after one's well-being; in these cases, all are permitted.
22. The Precept Regarding Teaching the Dharma to Nuns until Sunset.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
After Nanda had been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the nuns, he remained silent; Mahāprajāpatī requested him again, and he taught them until sunset.
The bhikṣuṇīs went out from the Jetavana and stayed overnight within the city moat, whereupon they were criticized by the laity.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha then rebuked them and established a rule:
"If a bhikṣu has been appointed by the Saṃgha to perform instruction or to perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) alone..."

When the Saṃgha appoints a teacher from among its members, it does so through a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman). A bhikṣuṇī, or even until sunset, who has been appointed by the Saṃgha to teach the nuns, must return before sunset.
Except for formal instruction, if one receives, recites, or inquires about the scriptures, or engages in other such matters until sunset;
or except for a *bhikṣuṇī*, if one receives the scriptures and so forth from a woman or any other person until sunset—all these constitute *duṣkṛta* (offenses of wrong-doing).
A *pāyattika* offense;
for a nun and others, it is a *dubbhāsita*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
When teaching nuns, one should cease before sunset;
except for women, one may teach others;
and if preaching at a ferry crossing, it is permissible if the nuns are listening of their own accord.
It is permitted if one preaches the Dharma at night with traveling merchants; or within a nunnery;
or if invited by someone and listens because the preaching occurs upon that occasion.
23. The Precept on Reviling the Instructor.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
When the nuns heard that the instructor was coming, they went out to welcome him and provide for his needs. The group of six [monks] became jealous and said:
"He is not sincere; he instructs the bhikṣuṇīs solely for the sake of food.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, He consequently established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus, 'The bhikṣus instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food,' it is a pāyattika offense."
If one speaks indistinctly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases:

The fact is indeed so: if one provides instruction for the sake of receiving food and drink as an offering; if one teaches, recites, or receives the scriptures, or answers questions, for the sake of food and drink;
or if one speaks playfully or erroneously—in all such cases, there is no offense.
24. The Precept Regarding Giving Robes to a Nun Who Is Not a Relative.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A bhikṣu who was fully endowed with dignified deportment was seen by a nun, who conceived a sense of faith and repeatedly invited him [to accept robes]. The bhikṣu, however, did not accept them.
Later, when the monks were distributing robes, they gave a robe to a nun, who accepted it immediately.
The monk resented and rebuked her, repeatedly speaking of it to others.
The bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha.
The Buddha prohibited this precept.
If a bhikṣu, as explained above regarding those who are not relatives,
[takes] a bhikṣuṇī’s robe— of the ten kinds mentioned above.
Except for trade, one may exchange clothing for clothing, or exchange it for non-clothing items, needles, knives, or even thread; down to as little as a single *jin* of medicinal herbs.
A *pāyattika* offense.
For *bhikṣuṇīs* and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one gives a robe to a relative nun, exchanges robes with one another, or gives them to a *stūpa*, to the Buddha, or to the Saṃgha.
25. The precept regarding making robes for a nun who is not a relative.

While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, Kālodāyin made a great robe for a nun; he then cut it into the shape of a phallus. Once completed, he gave it to her and instructed her to wear it at the rear of the assembly, which gave rise to the derision of the laity.
The nuns reported this transgression to the Buddha, and consequently, he established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika offense."
If that bhikṣu, according to how much he cuts with the knife, sews one stitch for every [cut], he falls [into an offense].

If he further opens it to look at it, pulls it, irons it, rubs it with his hand, or grasps the corners to pull them square and folds it neatly; or if he applies a border, seeks thread, or joins thread—in all such cases, it is a duṣkṛta (minor offense).
For nuns and others, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
making [a robe] for a relative nun;
If one makes it for the Saṃgha; or for a stūpa;
or if one borrows it and washes, dyes, or repairs it before returning it to the owner—all such cases are permitted.
26. The Precept Regarding Sitting with a Nun.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Kāḷudāyin and the nun Utpalavarṇā were both handsome; each harbored lustful intentions, and they sat together outside the gate.
The laypeople collectively took offense, using the analogy of a mandarin duck.
When the bhikṣus heard this report, the Buddha consequently established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu stays in the same place as a bhikṣuṇī—meaning one is a bhikṣu and the other is a bhikṣuṇī."
There are two kinds of concealment:
concealment by sight refers to when one cannot see due to dust, mist, smoke, clouds, or darkness;
concealment by hearing refers to when one does not even hear ordinary speech.
If there is an obstruction such as a tree, a wall, a fence, a garment, or any other object;
and if the person sitting in that place is the third person who is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind; or if they are standing—[in all these cases], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
A *pāyattika* offense;
for a nun and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
If a bhikṣu has a companion;
or if there is someone who knows [the situation], and there are two such persons who are neither blind nor deaf;
or if while walking he steps over and falls to the ground.
If one is ill;
if one is under the influence of superior force;
or if there are such calamities as those involving the King or Brahmins—all these are permitted.
27. The Precept on Traveling with Nuns.

While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus traveled through the countryside together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs. Householders criticized and disparaged them, and the bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha. The Buddha then rebuked them and established the rule.
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī, saying, "Let us go together to a certain village, city,
or country," and they travel along the same path— this refers to traveling through the designated boundaries between villages.
From one village to another village, according to the extent of the many boundaries, one falls [into an offense] for each.
If it is not a village, but one travels through an uninhabited place for up to ten *li*, one falls [into an offense].

If one village is omitted, or ten *li* are omitted, such that one travels through multiple villages within the same boundary, or if there is a concerted agreement for such travel, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
Except at other times, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Another time" refers to when traveling with merchants, or when there is suspicion that there may be bandits and thieves,
or fear and dread that there may be bandits and thieves;
this is called "another time."

For nuns and others, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if there was no prior agreement; if traveling with a large group; if traveling through a place of doubt or fear where going there results in safety; or if one is under the compulsion of force, or facing life-threatening dangers such as those involving the violation of the *brahmacarya*. These are all permitted.
28. The Precept Regarding Traveling on a Boat with a Bhikṣuṇī.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six bhikṣus traveled upriver and downriver on a boat together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, which caused the laypeople to collectively express their disapproval.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept:
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to board the same boat, whether going upriver or downriver, and they enter the boat together, he commits an offense of falling (pārājika).
Any other expedient means constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Except for crossing directly [the water], it is a *pāyattika* offense.
For nuns and others, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if there was no prior agreement,
or if one simply crosses to the other shore.
If one boards a boat, the boatman may lose his way, whether going upstream or downstream;
or one may fail to reach the opposite shore in safety;
or one may be held captive by forceful power.
There is no offense due to threats to life or threats to one's chastity.
Twenty-nine: The precept against eating food praised by a nun.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A lay devotee invited Śāriputra and others, having spread out fine seats in the open air;
when the nun Utpalavarṇā saw this, she falsely said, "Those who have been invited are all lowly and base."
"If I were to invite him, it would be Devadatta and his like—the dragons among dragons.
After he returned from eating, he recounted the full account, and the Buddha consequently rebuked him and established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu, whether knowing or not knowing [the circumstances], does so, he commits no offense."

A bhikṣuṇī praises and exhorts those who dwell in the forest (āraṇyaka), those who practice alms-gathering (piṇḍapātika), and even those who wear the three robes, recite verses, are learned, are Dharma-preachers, uphold the Vinaya, and practice meditation.
If one obtains food through specific conditions from dawn until midday and eats it—
except for food previously intended by a donor— one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
This means that with every swallow, one incurs a downfall.
Except for food and drink, if one receives robes for the body, oil for lamps, or other offerings as gifts, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
for a *bhikṣuṇī* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if one was unaware, if the donor had prior intention, if there was no thought of proselytizing, if the *bhikṣuṇī* acted on her own initiative, if the donor ordered the *bhikṣuṇī* to manage the matter, or if the food was given after begging without intentional proselytization.
30. The precept against traveling with a woman.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A wife and her mother-in-law quarreled, and she returned to Vaiśālī.
At that time, Anuruddha wished to go to that country, and this woman was to be his companion.
Her husband pursued them and caught them; he beat Anuruddha until his life-force was nearly severed.
The bhikṣu reported the matter to the Buddha, who then rebuked him and established this precept.
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman as described above to travel along the same path together, even for as far as a village, it is a pāyattika offense.
If they travel within the boundaries of a village, or if he travels with the four assemblies including the bhikṣuṇīs, it is all a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense if one was unaware beforehand, did not make a prior appointment, must go there to obtain peace, or if there are constraints such as forceful opposition or other difficulties.
Thirty-one: Receiving the precepts after exceeding the time limit for eating.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a village called Anāthapiṇḍada in the kingdom of Kośala, where a householder had built a residence and regularly provided a single meal.
The group of six monks frequently accepted these offerings, and the householder said:
"I have provided lodging for one night this week.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, he consequently established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation to a meal at a single location and stays there for one night..."
Regarding "food," it refers even to food taken at the proper time.
Regarding "one who is not ill" or "one who is ill," this refers to one whose illness is aggravated by staying in that village.
A bhikṣu should eat only once [a day].
If one receives more than this, for every swallow, there is an offense of *pāyattika*.
Apart from food, receiving other requisites such as robes, oil for lamps, and so forth, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; [if received beyond the limit], it is a *pāyattika*.
The same applies to nuns regarding the offense. There is no offense in the following cases: [if it was] received while staying overnight;
If one is ill, or has received excessive food;
or if a layperson invites one to stay, saying, "I have prepared this food for the sake of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya";
or if a donor invites one to a meal in regular succession.
If sons, daughters, sisters, or wives invite one in succession;
or if one accepts food from this person today and from that person tomorrow;
or if there are obstacles such as the interruption of travel and so forth.
32. The Precept Against Accepting an Invitation in Absentia.
The Buddha was traveling through the human realm from Rājagṛha when he arrived at the country of Aṇāpinḍada. Because of Śaṇu’s offering of gruel, he then permitted the consumption of gruel.
Because he ate thick congee, and because he accepted food sent by donors during festivals, and later accepted further invitations, the laity mocked and criticized him.
The Buddha, on account of this, established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu accepts successive invitations, it is considered an offense."
There are two kinds: invitations by turn of the Sangha and individual invitations.
As for food: boiled rice, parched grain flour, dry rice, and so forth.
Except at other times, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The exceptions are: when one is ill; when one is unable to eat a sufficient amount of fine food while remaining seated;

during the period of giving robes; for one month after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony if there is no *kaṭhina* robe in force, or for five months if there is a *kaṭhina* robe; or if there is further food or robes to be given.
This is called the proper time.
If one does not relinquish a prior invitation but accepts a subsequent invitation, for every swallow [of food], it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not relinquish a subsequent invitation but accepts a prior invitation, for every swallow, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases: when one is ill;
when robes are being distributed;

If one receives many invitations within a single day, one may accept one invitation for oneself and give the others away to others, saying: "Venerable sir, I must go there; I now bestow this upon you."

If one is given non-food, or if it is insufficient, or if there is no one to invite one to eat, or if one obtains food after having already eaten, or if there is both a preceding meal and a subsequent meal at the same location—in all such cases, it is permitted.
33. The Precept on Eating in a Separate Group.

When the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, Devadatta instructed others to harm the Buddha and further incited Ajātaśatru to kill his father; consequently, his ill repute spread abroad and his offerings were cut off, so that he went begging for alms with five bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who then rebuked them and established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu, apart from the community, [eats] with four or more persons—
'food' refers to rice, parched grain, boiled rice, and so forth."
Except at other times, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Other times" refers to when one is ill—even down to having a split in the heel of the foot;

when making robes; after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; during the month when there is no *kāṭhina* robe; during the five months when there is a robe; or even when making a single "horse-tooth" stitch upon a robe.
Regarding the giving of robes, it is the same as the preceding precept.
Regarding travel on land, it refers to coming and going within a distance of at least half a *yojana*.
Regarding travel by boat, it refers to boarding a boat to travel upstream or downstream for at least half a *yojana*.
When the great assembly gathers, even when there are only four people sufficient for the meal, having one person in excess is a source of trouble;
with five, ten, or even a hundred people, having one person in excess is likewise a source of trouble.
When a śramaṇa distributes food, those who are outside these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, namely other renunciants and those who have gone forth from non-Buddhist paths—
this is the proper time.
If there is no reason for taking food apart from the assembly, one should make a formal announcement, saying:
"I have no cause or condition for this food taken apart from the assembly; I wish to leave.
If others likewise have no reason, they too are permitted to leave.
If there are two or three people, they may eat as they please.
If there are four or more, they should divide themselves into two groups and enter the meal area alternately.
If there is a specific reason for one to join the group, they should immediately rise and announce it, saying:
“I have a reason for taking food apart from the assembly and wish to enter.
The Buddha said,
“You should enter according to the order of the senior monks.”
It is auspicious not to speak if there is a valid reason.
If one partakes of food with a separate group, for every swallow, a *pāyattika* offense is incurred.
The same applies to the *bhikṣuṇīs*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
those circumstances for which exceptions were fully enumerated above;
or if there are two or three persons; or if...
33. The precept against eating together;
if one says there is a cause or reason for going, it is permitted.
34. The precept against taking food from a woman returning home or from a merchant beyond the limit.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A woman, on her way back to her husband’s home, repeatedly gave food she had prepared to bhikṣus; because she delayed for a long time and did not return, her husband took another wife.
Furthermore, there were traveling merchants who gave away portions of their food as alms, which were subsequently plundered by thieves.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and he consequently established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson where there are both men and women present..."

If one requests a bhikṣu for cakes, parched grain, or boiled rice, and the bhikṣu requires them, he may accept two or three bowls; having returned to the monastery, he should divide them to be eaten with the other bhikṣus.
If one does not take food back, he informs the bhikṣus:
"In such-and-such a household there is food for a newly arrived wife, and there is provisions for merchants on the road; if you eat it, you should leave after eating;
if you take it back, it shall be limited to two or three bowls."
If they come carrying one or two bowls, he shall instruct them one by one, even saying: "You have already brought three bowls; be careful not to bring any more back."

If a bhikṣu, being not ill, [thinking] he cannot finish eating fine food while remaining seated in one place, receives more than two or three bowls and carries it back to the saṃghārāma, he commits a *pāyattika* offense upon exiting that gate; if he attempts it with the intention of repentance, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one eats alone without sharing the food with other bhikṣus, it is a *duṣkṛta*; [if one does so intentionally], it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not inquire of a woman returning from a journey or a merchant regarding food on the road, or if one does not inform the other bhikṣus, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
receiving two or three bowls;
or receiving more than that when ill.
Having asked [the donor], they shall divide [the goods] together so that he knows the location of the village;
if they personally deliver them to the nunnery, they may receive them;
if they are delivered to the nunnery and received there, there is no offense.
35. The Precept on Eating After Having Sufficient Food.
When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, he taught the practice of eating a single meal, requiring that one be fully satiated with five kinds of food.
Later, as they remained emaciated, the Buddha said, "I allow those who attend to the sick to eat the remains of the food of the patient.
He further permitted the "procedure for leftover food" (*kṛtapiṇḍapāta*).
Because there were those with gluttonous appetites who did not know the proper rules for eating, he consequently established this precept.

If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal, should at any time accept an invitation and eat from among the five kinds of staple foods—whether it be rice, parched grain, boiled rice, or the like—and eats until he is fully satiated.
If one has not performed the *kṛta-śeṣa-kalpa* (the ritual for leftover food), they take the food back and perform the ritual, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
I have already eaten my fill; I recognize this and observe this; please perform the ritual for leftover food."
Having taken a small portion of food himself, he should say to him:
"I have had enough;
you take this and eat it."
If one eats what has been prepared by another, it is a *pāyattika*. Within this,
for each of the acts of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, there are distinct categories of offenses, as fully detailed in the *Vinaya*.
There are *dhaññabhojana* foods: those consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, oils, sesame, black rock-honey, and finely ground powders.
If that bhikṣu, having already finished eating, accepts and eats food without performing the *kṛtākṛta* (remaining-food) ritual, he commits an offense for every swallow.
If he eats after another has finished, or if he knows that another has finished eating and still eats, [he likewise commits an offense].
Taking food with one's own hand;
placing food on the ground; having a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) prepare it.
If one performs it in front of a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food); or if one performs it by covering it with unwholesome food;
or if one carries it away—in all these cases, the *atirikta-bhakti-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food) is not established, and it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For the four assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs,
it is a duṣkṛta offense. There is no offense in cases where one perceives food as non-food while eating.
Not accepting the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the practice of receiving food after the meal has been concluded); the prohibitory rules are the reverse of the above;
and if one is ill, one does not perform the formal ritual.
If one consumes the leftover food of a sick person without performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā* (the ritual for remaining food), it is an offense;
however, if the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā* has already been performed, there is no offense.
Thirty-six: Exhorting another to commit the offense of eating after having finished a meal.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

There were two brothers who had both become bhikṣus; one of them was gluttonous and fond of food, not knowing whether he had eaten enough or not, nor whether he had finished his meal or not, yet he would eat whatever he obtained.
He reproached him for that fault.
This [other] monk harbored resentment; seeing the former eat, he forcibly urged him to eat and again reproached him for the fault.
When the bhikṣu reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently established the precept.
If a bhikṣu knows [that he has already eaten], there is no offense for not knowing.
When another bhikṣu has finished eating, there are five kinds of food as mentioned above.
If one accepts an invitation, there are likewise five kinds as mentioned above.
If one does not perform the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food) and earnestly invites another to eat, saying, "Venerable One!

Take this food," then by reason of this—and no other—if the recipient previously did not know [of the rule] and lacked the perception that it was insufficient to eat, and if [the donor] gives it [to him] and he discards it;
[this constitutes an offense].
If one causes another to be raised up;
if one sends another to be given away;
or if one causes that which has not yet been enacted as a rule to be enacted as a rule.
If it is the leftover food of a sick person;
or if the food has already been consecrated by ritual, one must not cause another to commit an offense.
If one intends to cause another to commit an offense and the other accepts and eats it, both incur a *pārājika* offense with every swallow.

If one gives food and the recipient discards it; or if the recipient accepts it and sets it aside; or if the recipient accepts it and gives it to another person; or if the recipient, having accepted it, performs the ritual for eating (kappiya-kamma);
or if it is food from a sick person intended to cause another to commit an offense;

or if one gives the remains of a sick person's food; or if one gives food after performing the ritual for "leftover food" (vighasa-kamma) with the intent to cause another to commit an offense—under all such circumstances as these, giving [the food] constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
A *pāyattika* offense.
For the four assemblies, including the *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Thirty-seven: The precept against eating at improper times.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, during a popular festival, the two Śākya sons Nanda and Upananda went together to watch the performances and received food and drink; they returned to the mountain at dusk.
Kālodāyin entered the city at night to beg for alms; a woman saw him amidst the thunder and lightning and cried out, "A ghost!
A ghost!"
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu [eats] at an improper time—'improper time' meaning from the appearance of dawn until midday; this period is defined as the proper time according to the Dharma."
The food of the four continents is likewise.
Regarding "improper time," it refers to the period from midday until the sun has not yet risen the following morning.
There are two kinds of food to be received: *khādya* (solid food), as described above, and *bhojya* (soft food), which consists of five types of food, also as described above.
To eat [it] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one eats food received at an improper time, there is a downfall for every swallow.
If it is "at an improper time" and the improper time has passed, or if it is "for seven days" and the seven-day period has passed, there is likewise a downfall.
Regarding medicines to be taken for as long as one lives, to consume them without a valid reason constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in cases where it is done according to the method for preparing black stone honey (*khaṇḍa*).
If one who is ill takes emetic or purgative medicine and the prescribed time has passed, they may boil barley so that the husks do not break, strain the juice, and drink it.
Furthermore, there is no offense if the substance is expectorated from the throat rather than swallowed.
38. The Precept Regarding Eating Leftover Food from the Previous Night.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
Kāla was practicing dhyāna; exhausted by the fatigue of begging for alms, he ate whatever he had obtained first.
A bhikṣu did not see [a certain monk] at the morning or midday meal; he searched for him and related the circumstances in detail.
When the bhikṣu informed the Buddha, the Buddha rebuked him, saying:
"Although you have few desires, you act according to the customs of later generations."
Thereupon, he established this precept:

"If a bhikṣu has received [food] that was stored overnight and then receives it again today, until the following day, all śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas who have received full ordination, shall be considered impure."
There are two kinds of food:
non-primary food consists of root-food up to fine flour-food;
primary food consists of rice, parched grain, and so on, up to meat.
Regarding "eating": to eat food that has been kept overnight, one falls into an offense with every swallow.
To eat beyond the limits of the "non-timely" period or the "seven-day" period also constitutes a fall.
To consume a medicine for life without a cause or condition of illness is a *duṣkṛta* (transgression).
This is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
giving food that was received overnight to one's parents;
If laborers are building a stupa or a dwelling and have been paid according to their wages, and a bhikṣu who is begging for food subsequently obtains food from those laborers;
or if food has entered the cracks and crevices of his alms bowl, he may wash it according to the Dharma, and if the remainder does not come out, he may keep it.
If one has previously received ghee or oil for nasal irrigation, if it comes out with the saliva, it may be discarded;
the remainder may be used. Thirty-nine: The precept against accepting food.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

The city dwellers, for the sake of their parents and others, performed sacrifices and made offerings at crossroads and even in shrines; when bhikṣus who wore rag-robes and lived on alms took this food for themselves, the householders were all filled with resentment.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who then established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu eats food that has not been received and not given, it constitutes 'not having received' [the food].
There are five kinds of receiving:"
Giving with the hand and receiving with the hand;
giving with the hand and receiving by holding an object;
giving by holding an object and receiving with the hand.
If one gives by holding an object and receives by holding an object;

or if one passes an object from a distance, such that both the giver and the receiver are aware of it and there is no contact or obstruction between them until it falls into the hand—this constitutes [a valid reception].
Furthermore, there are five kinds:

giving by means of the body, clothing, a bent elbow, or a vessel; receiving with the aforementioned four methods; or, if there is a specific cause or condition, placing it on the ground to give—these constitute the five kinds.
Regarding the consumption of *khādaniya* (solid foods):
from roots up to powdered flour.
It is also said:
Rice, roasted flour, dry rice, and so forth;
as for medicinal substances that are considered *sappi-anna* (food), these are ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.
If one places them in the mouth and, without being given food, takes them into the mouth by oneself, for every swallow, it constitutes an offense.
If one exceeds the limit of "improper time" or the "seven-day period," one likewise falls into an offense.
To consume a medicine for life-long use without receiving it when there is no valid reason constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Except for water and tooth-sticks, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
One who does not commit an offense takes pure water and tooth-sticks.
If one does not receive clarified butter or oil for nasal irrigation and they exit together with saliva, there is no offense regarding the remainder.

If food is picked up by a bird or blown into a begging bowl by the wind while a bhikṣu is on his almsround, he may remove that food—even if it requires removing as much as a fingernail—and there is no offense regarding what remains.
40. The Precept Against Soliciting Delicate Food.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Upāli’s brother, Nanda, had a merchant as a donor (dānapati), to whom he said:
"I wish to have some mixed food.
The merchant leader asked,
"What ailment makes you think of this?"
He replied, "I have no affliction; it is merely a desire of my mind.
The merchants criticized and disparaged him.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who then rebuked them and established a precept:

"If a bhikṣu obtains fine foods—milk, curd, fish, or meat—and if that bhikṣu is not ill, he must not eat such fine foods until the end of a single sitting, even if he is ill. (For one who is ill, it is permitted.)
If one seeks [a robe] for oneself, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
The sick person begs for it themselves;
they beg for it on behalf of the sick and eat what is obtained;
or they do so for another.
He acts for his own sake;
if he obtains food without begging, there is no offense.
Forty-one: The precept against giving food to non-Buddhists.
The Buddha, leading his disciples, traveled from Kosala to Śrāvastī.
The Buddha and the community of monks received a great abundance of cakes and food, which he instructed Ānanda to distribute to other beggars.
He then gave the sticky rice cakes to the woman.
Furthermore, because an outsider had obtained food, it was called "obtained by the shaven-headed layman.
The Buddha assembled the Sangha and informed them of what he had heard, subsequently establishing this precept.

If a bhikṣu [associates with] male followers of external paths, female followers of external paths, naked ascetics of heterodox schools, or pāṣaṇḍas—these are those who have gone forth outside this community.
"To give with one's own hand" means to place it on the ground to give, or to have another person give it.
"To give food" refers to *khajjaka* (hard foods), such as root-foods up to fruit-foods; or oil-foods up to finely ground powdered foods.
The five kinds of food are also as described above. [If one eats them at the improper time, it is] a pāyattika offense;
for nuns and others, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

There is no offense if the gift is abandoned and placed on the ground before being given, if one causes another to give it, if it is given to one's parents, if it is given as the price for food for those working at a stūpa or a separate dwelling, or if it is forcibly seized by means of power. There is no offense in these cases.
42. The Precept Regarding Visiting Other Families Before or After Meals.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

A householder prepared a meal for the Saṃgha on behalf of Baddhālinda; however, he arrived only when it was nearly time for the meal to be over, and the bhikṣus had finished eating before he could provide enough food.
Furthermore, a high minister in the city of Rājagṛha attained the fruits of the path and instructed Baddhananda to distribute [the food] among the Saṃgha;
however, after finishing his meal, he went to other households.
The bhikṣus reported these two transgressions, and the Buddha established this dual precept.
If a bhikṣu, having previously accepted an invitation, goes to another household—
where men and women reside— either before the morning meal when the dawn has appeared until the time for eating, or after the morning meal from the time for eating until midday.
If one does not entrust [one's bedding] to another bhikṣu, or if staying alone in a single room, one fails to entrust it to a fellow resident living nearby within the same boundary,
it constitutes a pāyattika offense, except during other [permitted] times.
"Other times" refers to the time of illness, as described above;
the time of making robes, also as described above;
and the time of receiving robes: for one who has no robes, it is for one month after the *pravāraṇā*; for one who has robes, it is for five months.
Apart from these occasions, it refers to those times when one encourages others to prepare food or offers robes as a gift;
this is what is meant by "the proper time.

If, after having previously accepted an invitation, one eats before or after [the meal] without having made a formal announcement (*anujñāpana*), and enters the gate, one commits an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*).
Any other expedient means constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in cases where the aforementioned exemptions apply.
One should entrust oneself to a bhikṣu;

if no bhikṣu is available, one may go without having made such an entrustment to the storehouse, to a dwelling on the edge of a village, or to a nunnery; or one may go to the house where one has been entrusted.
If many families spread out sitting mats and invite bhikṣus, it is permitted if there are difficult circumstances.
Forty-three: The precept against sitting forcefully in a family home.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Kālodāyin had a former lay friend’s wife who was a *upāsikā* observing the fast; both were handsome and mutually infatuated with one another.
Later, when he went to her house, the woman had adorned herself, for her husband was exceedingly fond of her.
After the bhikṣu had finished eating and remained seated, his husband became angry and departed.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha consequently established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu stays with a man who takes women as food, or a woman who takes men as food."
The house is as described above.
Within it are treasures: carnelian, agate, pearl, amber, gold, and silver.
One who sits down forcefully should extend their hand until it reaches the door before sitting. One should sit in this manner.
A *pāyattika* offense.
If one is both blind and deaf, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
If the householder has jewels, and [the monk] sits within reach of hand at the door;
or if there are two bhikṣus as companions;
or if there is a person capable of discerning [the situation], or a guest in the same place, who is neither blind nor deaf; [in these cases, it is permissible].
Or, having passed through it previously, one does not abide;
or a disease breaks out and causes one to fall to the ground;
or one is sustained by the power of another.
Or if one is bound;
or due to life-threatening or *brahman*-threatening dangers—there is no offense.
Forty-fourth: The precept against sitting in secret with a family.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

Kālodāyin, recollecting a previous precept stating that "one should sit where one’s hand can reach the door," sat behind a door-panel and conversed with a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) who had come for the *poṣadha* ceremony.
The bhikṣus heard these words and, censuring [the conduct], reported it to the Buddha. Consequently, he rebuked them and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu is in a household where there is treasure, it shall be as in the previous precept."
In a screened place— whether by a tree, wall, partition, fence, or lattice, or by a cloth or other object that acts as a screen—
if one sits [so as to be seen], it is a *pāyattika*.
If one is in a house where food is being served, one must extend one's hand [to the door] so that the bhikṣu seeking alms may see [the donor].
The remaining details regarding the definition of the offense and the opening of the conditions are the same as for the preceding precepts.
Forty-five: The precept against sitting alone with a woman in an open space.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Kālodayin sat together with the female lay follower Ciñcā in the open air. A bhikṣu who was begging for alms saw this and felt disdain for it; he reported the matter in detail to the other bhikṣus.
They brought the transgression to the Buddha's attention, and consequently, the Buddha established a precept.
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a single woman—
a human female possessing intelligence whose life-faculty is not severed— in an open space,
that is to say, in a place where he may be seen or heard while remaining out of sight.
Pāyattika. The definition of the offense and the exemptions are both as in the preceding precept.
Forty-six: The precept on driving another out of a settlement.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Upananda had quarreled with a bhikṣu and harbored a grudge in his heart.
He then led him into a part of the city where there was no food; knowing that the time for the meal at the Jetavana had already passed, he said:
“You great evildoer! You have prevented me from obtaining food!
Depart at once!
Thus deprived of food, he became utterly exhausted.
A bhikṣu reported this transgression, and as a result, the Buddha rebuked him and established the precept: "If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir, let us go together to a village; there are four kinds of villages, as described above.'"
"I shall give you food," he said, and at that time [the other] ate.
Yet that bhikṣu did not ultimately instruct [his companion] to give the food to this bhikṣu, but instead said: "Go away!

I do not enjoy sitting or speaking in your company; I enjoy sitting and speaking alone. For this reason, if through such means he abandons the place where he was seen and goes to a place where he is heard, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The same applies to acting as intermediaries for one another.
Only when both seeing and hearing are avoided does one incur the offense of *pāyattika*.
If it is not through other expedient means that one sends the person away, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one gives food and sends [the person] away;
or if [the person] is ill; or if they lack dignified deportment such that people are displeased upon seeing them, and one personally brings food to give to them.
If they have broken the precepts and so forth;
or if there is a threat to life or to the Brahma-faring, one may employ skillful means to send them away,
but not out of malice or resentment.
47. The Precept on Medicines Beyond the Limit. When the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, Mahānāman invited the Saṃgha to receive medicine.

Because the group of six monks harbored resentment, they sought out medicines that were difficult to obtain; he then went to the market to procure them for them, whereupon they reviled him and cut off the Saṃgha’s supply of medicine.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu, during the four months of the summer retreat,
provides medicine,"— the "condition" refers to an invitation for medicine.
When a healthy bhikṣu becomes ill, he may accept the medicine prescribed by a physician;
he should accept it.
If he accepts more than that, or if it is at night, or if there is a fixed limit to the medicine, he may accept it during the four months of the summer retreat.
If there is no fixed limit regarding the time of night, one may accept [the medicine] whenever it is offered, regardless of the medicinal divisions.
This excludes cases of regular invitations or when a person says, "I shall always provide you with medicine."
Regarding the "further invitation" (*punar-yācanā*): once [the medicine] has been refused, one may subsequently invite [the donor] again and give it to them.
Regarding the "invitation for distribution" (*vibhāga-yācanā*): one takes the medicine to the monastery and distributes it among the community.
Regarding the "invitation for as long as life lasts" (*yāvaj-jīva-yācanā*): [the donor says], "I shall provide medicine for as long as my life endures."
A *pāyattika*. Non-offenses are as previously exempted.
Forty-eight: The Precept on Viewing an Army.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
When the people rose in rebellion, the King led his sixfold army to campaign against them; the group of six monks went to observe the battle lines.
When King Prasenajit saw this, he was displeased. He offered a package of honey to the Buddha and, holding it, paid homage with a prostration.
He went to where the Buddha was and related these circumstances in detail; consequently, the Buddha rebuked him and established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu goes to view an army array, whether it be at play or in combat."
An "army" refers to even a single horse, a single chariot, or a single foot-soldier.
Except in cases of specific circumstances, if there is a need for a formal announcement or if one is summoned by invitation, [one must not enter].
It is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not avoid it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
From the lower to the higher, from the path to the non-path, if one does not see [the danger], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies to not seeing [the person] through skillful means;
if one sees them, it is an offense of falling (pāyattika).
There is no offense in the following cases:
If one goes for a specific purpose;
if one is invited to go;
or if one is taken away by force;
If one has already set out ahead while the army arrives later, one should leave the road to avoid it.

If the path by water or land is cut off, or there is danger from wild beasts or bandits, or the waters have risen high, or if one is bound by forceful power, or if there is a life-threatening peril such as a threat to one's religious life (brahmacarya), there is no offense in not leaving the road.
Forty-nine: The precept against staying overnight in an army camp.
While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks had a reason to go and stay overnight in an army camp. A householder said:
"We have these [ears] only because of desire; what does a śramaṇa need with them?
The bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established a precept.
If a bhikṣu has a legitimate reason, he is permitted to stay within an army for two or three nights;
if he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika offense.
There is no offense if he stays for two nights, and on the third night, before the dawn has appeared, he moves beyond the range of hearing and sight.
If the path by water or land is cut off due to life-threatening dangers or obstacles to the Brahma-faring, and one does not separate [from the object], there is no offense.
Fifty: The Precept on Observing a Battle.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

The group of six monks had a reason to be with an army and were watching the combat prowess; one among them was struck by an arrow, and his companions carried him away on a cloth-bier, which the householder saw and found strange.
When the bhikṣus heard this report, the Buddha consequently established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu stays within an army for two or three nights, or at any time observes battle arrays, or observes the military maneuvers, elephants, horses, or forces of an army, it is a pāyattika."
The remainder is as clarified in the preceding precepts.
Fifty-one: The Precept Against Drinking Alcohol.
The Buddha was staying in the country of Cīda.
Sagata served as the Buddha’s attendant; he went to the chamber of a matted-hair Brahmin who lived among the nāgas and stayed there overnight, whereupon he subdued the nāga during the night.
At dawn, he presented it to King Kauśāmbī.
Later, while traveling through that country, he gave him black liquor, and [the man] fell drunk upon the road.
After the Buddha had explained the ten faults of drinking alcohol, he established the precept:

"If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol—whether it be wood-wine, rice wine made from non-glutinous rice, rice wine made from other grains, barley wine, or any other substance used to make wine—it is all prohibited."
This is a *pāyattika*.
If it is an intoxicant that lacks the color, fragrance, or taste of an intoxicant;
or if it is not an intoxicant but possesses the color, fragrance, or taste of an intoxicant—in neither case may it be drunk.
If one cooks, mixes, eats, or drinks alcohol, one falls into [a grave offense].
If one drinks sweet-flavored alcohol or sour-flavored alcohol, or eats yeast or dregs of wine, all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).
The three phrases regarding perception and doubt constitute an offense.
There is no offense if one has an illness that is not cured by other medicines, and thus uses alcohol as medicine.
If one applies alcohol to a wound—there is no offense in any case.
Fifty-two: The precept against sporting in water.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
While the group of seventeen was playing and splashing water in the Ajiravatī River, King Seniya Bimbisāra and Queen Mallikā saw them from atop their palace.
The King said, "Look at those whom you serve!"
The lady said, "He has only recently left the household life; perhaps he is foolish and ignorant.
She then offered rock honey to the Buddha, whereupon the Buddha rebuked her and established a precept.

If a bhikṣu plays in the water, indulging his whims and acting wantonly, moving from here to there, going against the current or with the current, diving in here and surfacing there, splashing water with his hands, or even playing by filling his bowl with water.
A *pāyattika*. With the exception of water, if one plays with curd-milk, fermented grain-liquor, or barley-gruel in a vessel, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
If one is traveling on a road and crosses water;
or goes from this shore to the other shore;
or uses bamboo or wood dragged by the water to go up or down with the current; [in such cases, there is no offense].
If one picks up stones or sand;
or if an object is lost and sinks to the bottom of the water, causing it to submerge here and emerge there;
or if, while practicing the art of swimming, one raises one's arms and splashes or spatters the water—there is no offense.
53. The Precept on Prodding Others.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
One member of the group of six monks prodded one member of the group of seventeen monks, nearly causing him to die.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu strikes or tickles another with his fingers—
the ten fingers of the hands or feet— it is a pāyattika."
Excluding the hands and feet, if one strikes or prods with a staff, a fly-whisk handle, a door key, or any other object,
it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). There is no offense if it was not done intentionally.
If one is asleep, touching them causes them to awaken.
If one is walking in or out, or sweeping the ground, there is no offense if they inadvertently touch another with the tip of a staff.
Fifty-four: The precept against not accepting admonition.
The Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī.
Chanda intended to violate the precepts, and a bhikṣu admonished him, saying:
"Do not harbor such thoughts; you ought not to do so."
If one does not follow the admonitions of others, one immediately commits various offenses.
A bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked him and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika."
If another person forbids one by saying, "Do not do this; you should not act thus," yet one intentionally proceeds to do so, one commits a root offense (*mūlāpatti*);
because one did not follow their words, there is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one knows for oneself, "What I am doing is wrong," yet proceeds to do it intentionally, one commits a root offense;
if one does not comply with the verbal admonition, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense if, when an ignorant person comes to admonish one, one replies:
"You may ask your teacher or preceptor; once you have further studied, recited the scriptures, and understood the methods of admonition, you may employ them when giving counsel.
There is no offense if one speaks thus in jest, while speaking to oneself, or while speaking in a dream, or if intending to say one thing, one says another instead.
55. Fear of the Bhikṣu Precepts.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
Nāgapāla attended upon the Buddha at his side.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they are walking in meditation, those who wish to make offerings stand at the head of the path.
Those men, during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, requested the Buddha to return; they then turned their robes backward and brandished their staffs, intending to terrify the Buddha.
At dawn the next day, he assembled the Sangha and consequently established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu terrifies another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one uses form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, or mental objects to terrify another person, whether that person is terrified or not, each instance constitutes a downfall."
If he does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he speaks of the terrors of the six sense objects, such as forms and sounds, and his speech is intelligible, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is unintelligible, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases:

if it is dark and there is no light; if it is a place for defecating or urinating; if one fears wild beasts, mistaking them for something else; or if one is terrified by the sound of footsteps, coughing, or the sound of contact;
or if one displays forms and such to others without the intention to cause fear.

If such signs truly exist—for instance, if one dreams of imminent death, of leaving the monastic life, or of losing property; or if one’s preceptor, parents, or others suffer from serious illness or die—one may speak to them to inform them.
Whether this is done intentionally or by mistake, there is no offense in any case.
56. The Precept Regarding Bathing More Than Once Every Half-Month.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
There was a pond in the Bamboo Grove where King Bimbisāra permitted the bhikṣus to bathe regularly.

During the latter part of the night, the group of six monks entered the pond to bathe. The king, accompanied by his court ladies, arrived at the pond and encountered them; the king did not bathe at all, which caused the ministers to feel resentment and indignation.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established a precept.
If a bhikṣu bathes once every half-month, a bhikṣu who is not ill should accept this; he must not exceed it. Bathing within the interval of half a month is what is meant by "exceeding."
Except at other times, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Other times" refers to the heat of the season— the forty-five days following spring and the first month of summer—
or the time of illness, down to the point where the body becomes foul-smelling.
Regarding the time of performance: it includes at least sweeping the ground in front of one's house;
regarding the time of wind and rain: it includes at least a single whirlwind or a single drop of rain falling upon the body;
regarding the time of traveling on the road: it includes at least half a yojana, whether coming or going.
This is the proper time.
If one bathes beyond this limit, whether the entire body or half the body is submerged, it constitutes a downfall;
if one employs skillful means to repent, it is a *duṣkṛta* (transgression).
There is no offense in cases where there is an allowance as previously mentioned for washing frequently, or when one is compelled by forceful power to wash.
Fifty-seven: The precept against lighting fires in the open air.
The Buddha was staying at the city of Khānumata.
The group of six said to one another,
"We may not speak as we please in the presence of the Elder.
They immediately went out onto the open ground, gathered various twigs and grasses, and lit a fire toward him.
A poisonous snake was within the robes; its fiery breath forced it out, whereupon it leaped in terror and threw fire, burning the Buddha’s lecture hall.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently rebuked them and established a precept.
If a bhikṣu, being without illness, or even when ill, lights a fire on open ground for his own use or to warm himself,
or instructs another to do so, except under specific circumstances, it is a pāyattika offense.
If he burns anything in an open space—whether grass, wood, branches, leaves, hemp, kusa grass, or cow dung, husks, excrement, or chaff—it is a pāyattika offense.
If one places fire within grass, wood, or even cow dung, it constitutes an offense.
If one throws something that has been half-burnt or charred into the fire, or onto burning coals, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one does not say to the person before them, "Know this; look at this," it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if one says, "Know this; look at this."
If the patient lights it himself, or instructs another to light it;
or if, due to certain circumstances, the caregiver cooks gruel, soup, or rice;
or if [the fire] is in a kitchen or a bathhouse;
Incensing the alms bowl, boiling dye, lighting lamps, and burning incense—none of these constitute an offense.
Fifty-eight: The precept against concealing another’s clothing or belongings.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A lay devotee invited the monks; the group of seventeen, carrying their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases, paced back and forth on one side, looking about as they wandered.
At that time, the group of six waited for their backs to turn, seized their belongings, and hid them.
The bhikṣus observed this and reported the transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu hides another bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case—whether hiding it himself or instructing another to hide it—even if done merely in jest, it is a pāyattika offense."
There is no offense in the following cases:
if one knows the object and picks it up after examining its characteristics;
or if it is in an open space and has been blown away or soaked by wind and rain, and one picks it up.
If the owner stores items negligently and they are left in disarray, one may store them for the sake of admonishing him;
if one has borrowed another's robes and the owner fails to take care of them, one may set them aside for fear of loss;
or if, on account of these robes, bowls, or other belongings, there is danger from life-threatening or spiritual obstacles (brahmacarya), one may store them—in all such cases, there is no offense.
Fifty-nine: The precept against taking clothing without permission from a truly pure donor.

When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks took the robes of a monk who was close and intimate with a truly pure donor after [the donor] had already given them; subsequently, they took and wore them without informing the owner.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, and later takes it back and wears it without informing the owner, it is a pāyattika."
There is no offense in the following cases:
taking what is given as a true gift; taking what is offered by the owner;
or taking what has been passed along in succession as a gift, according to one's own will.
60. The Precept on Wearing Garments.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks went about wearing white garments, which caused the householders to criticize and disparage them:
“There is no true Dharma such as that of kings and ministers!
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, he established this precept:
“If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe—whether it is a new robe by nature or the first one he has received from another.”
One should apply three types of discolored dyes, applying each color as desired:
either blue, black, or madder-brown.
The *Vinaya* commentary states:
Regarding this term "purified" (*śuddha*):
if it refers to dyeing a cloth, it is called "purified";
if it refers to a garment already made from purified cloth, it is called "purified" because one must mark it by placing a different-colored object in one spot as a sign.
From this point downward, whether it be clothing or non-clothing, these are items not currently in use; all such things should be marked with a dot as a sign of purification before being kept.
As for what is called "heavy," it refers to *kambala* (woolen blankets) and *karpāsa* (cotton cloth), which are considered the most important among garments.
If a bhikṣu wears any other new robe without having dyed it with one of the three kinds of discolored colors—either blue, black, or madder—he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one wears three kinds of robes without performing the ritual of marking them (kālakalpa), one falls into an offense.
If one wears heavy or light garments without performing the ritual of marking them, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If they are not robes—such as a bowl bag, a sandal bag, a needle-and-thread bag, a meditation belt, a waistband, a hood, a sun-shade cloth, or a cloth for wrapping sandals—and one keeps them without performing the ritual of purification, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one entrusts an unstained robe to the house of a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense if one obtains a robe from a layperson to be dyed in three colors; furthermore, there is no offense regarding minor or major items, nor when one keeps a cloth after performing the ritual purification (*śuddhi*).
61. The Precept Against Killing Animals Deliberately.
When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Kālodāyin took no pleasure in seeing crows; he shot one with a bamboo bow and killed it, whereupon it grew into a massive carcass.
When a lay devotee prostrated, he saw [the monks] doing so together and felt disdain for it.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and the Buddha consequently established a precept.

If a bhikṣu, at a time when other bhikṣus were sitting, rising, walking, or coming and going, intentionally kills many small insects, some may perform a *pāyattika* confession while others remain cautious; regarding this, the Buddha said:
"If one does not know, there is no offense.
This refers to killing whether by cutting with one's own hand or by commanding another to cut;
it concerns animals that are incapable of transformation.
If one [kills] a living being, it is a *pāyattika*.
The same offense applies to a bhikṣuṇī.
The exceptions are as in the "killing a human being" precept.
62. The Precept on Drinking Water Containing Insects.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks took water containing various insects and drank it, which led householders to criticize and resent them.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu, whether knowing or not knowing that there are insects, [uses water], he does not commit an offense.
Once the water has been cleared of insects, the same offense applies to drinking or using mixed insect-infused drinks, fermented grain wine, clear curd-liquor, or barley-water."
If there are insects [in the water] and one drinks it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*). There is no offense in the following cases:
If one did not know beforehand;
if there was no perception of insects;
or if the insects were large and moved away upon contact with the water.
If one strains water before drinking it, there is no offense.
Sixty-three: The precept against causing doubt and distress to a bhikṣu.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of seventeen addressed the group of six, saying, "How does one enter the first dhyāna?
and so on, up to "How does one attain the fruit of arhatship?
To which they replied:
"By saying what you have said, you have already committed a *pārājika* offense.
He went to other bhikṣus and questioned them; they then rebuked him, and because of this, the Buddha established the precept.
If a bhikṣu, at a time when many bhikṣus have gathered in one place to discuss the Dharma and Vinaya together,
departs with a mind full of doubt, thinking, "The bhikṣus are causing me doubt."
The Buddha said:
"If one does not act intentionally, there is no offense.

Regarding the troubling of another bhikṣu, or the suspicion of troubling him: it may be for the sake of [his] birth, his age, his receiving of the precepts, a formal ritual (karmavācanā), an offense, or the Dharma."
If she causes [the other] to be unhappy for even a brief moment, it is a *pāyattika*.
The same offense applies to a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*). There is no offense in the following cases:

The fact is indeed so; it was not done intentionally. Fearing that he might later feel doubt or regret for having accepted the offerings and the respectful salutations of others without cause, [the donor] says to him:
"You were not born at such a time; as other people are born, you know that you were not born at such a time.

The fact is indeed so; he has not lived for that many years. Fearing that he might later feel doubt or regret for receiving the offerings and honors of others, [the donor] says: "You have not lived for that many years."
"Like other bhikṣus, they know that you have not yet reached such an age";

this fact is indeed so. If one is less than twenty years of age and the assembly is separate within the boundary, fearing later doubt or regret regarding the acceptance of offerings and reverential salutations, one tells them to let [the candidate] know, so that he may return to his original place and receive the precepts again;

this fact is indeed so. If the motion (*jñapti*) is not accomplished and the formal act (*karman*) is not accomplished, it is an illegal separate assembly; fearing later doubt or regret regarding the acceptance of offerings and reverential salutations, one tells them to let [the candidate] know, so that he may return to his original place and receive the precepts again.

The fact is indeed so: having committed an offense ranging from *pārājika* down to *durbhāṣita*, he fears that others might later harbor doubts or regrets regarding his acceptance of offerings, or that monks who uphold the precepts might pay him homage; wishing therefore to make them know that he has repented according to the Dharma, he speaks of his offenses down to the *durbhāṣita*.
Furthermore, because he is coarse by nature and does not understand speech, he says: "What you have said is to claim for yourself the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*)."
If there is a mistake or if it is done in jest, there is no offense.
Sixty-fourth: The precept concerning concealing a bhikṣu’s offense.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Bhadananda was a close friend of the bhikṣu; having repeatedly committed offenses, he would say to him, "I have not told anyone.
Later, when they were fighting, Bhadananda said, "You have committed an offense," and added, "I cannot bear it any longer, so I am telling you."
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha,
who then rebuked them and established a rule: "If a bhikṣu, whether knowing it or not,
[reports] another bhikṣu’s grave offense— namely, one of the four pārājikas or a saṃghāvaśeṣa— he commits no offense."
Regarding concealment: if one knows that another has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), if one knows it during the morning meal, one must confess it after the meal;
if one knows it after the meal, one must confess it by the first watch of the night;
if one knows it during the first watch, one must confess it by the middle watch. In all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* (transgression).
If one knows [the offense] at midnight and, reaching the latter part of the night, intends to confess it but fails to do so until the dawn sign appears, it is a *pāyattika*.
This excludes concealing a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); it refers to concealing other offenses, or concealing one's own offense.
Except for a bhikṣuṇī, to conceal the offenses of others constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;
all other cases are *duṣkṛta*.
Bhikṣuṇīs commit the same offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
if one did not know beforehand;
or if one did not perceive it as a grave offense.
If one speaks it to another;
if no one speaks it to oneself;
or if one resolves to speak it and the dawn has already appeared;
If there is danger to life or to one's status as a Brahma-king, there is no offense.
Sixty-five: Ordaining those under the required age for full ordination.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
There was a group of seventeen youths, the eldest being seventeen years old and the youngest eleven, who left the household life out of faith.
The bhikṣus immediately ordained them and conferred upon them full ordination (upasampadā).
Unable to endure eating but once a day, he wept at night.
The Buddha awoke, learned of the situation, and after the night had passed, assembled the Sangha and established a formal rule and precept:
"When one has reached twenty years of age, one should receive the full ordination."
The Buddha said:
"If one has not yet reached twenty years of age, they cannot endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, rain, mosquitoes, gadflies, venomous insects, or harsh words;
nor can they endure physical pain and suffering."
Furthermore, one who is unable to maintain the precepts or subsist on a single meal [is not fit];
if one has reached twenty years of age, one is capable of enduring the various hardships mentioned above.
If a bhikṣu knows or does not know [the other's incapacity], there is no offense.
If one who is less than twenty years of age receives the full precepts, this person does not obtain the precepts.
That bhikṣu is to be rebuked for his folly; it is a pāyattika offense.
