If the person receiving the precepts knows they have not reached the required age, and the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the Sangha also know this, yet when asked within the assembly, "Have you reached the required age?", they reply that they have either reached it or not; or if they are doubtful, or do not know, or remain silent, or if the Sangha does not ask at all.
Within this, there are four cases:
if one knows or suspects [the offense], the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* and the community commits a *duṣkṛta*;
if one asserts otherwise or does not know, neither commits an offense.
If the three *karmavācanās* have been completed, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika*.

If it is during the interval, or if the formal motion (*jñapti*) has not yet been completed, or if he is merely preparing the means, or if he has shaved the hair, or if he has assembled the Sangha—the preceptor incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense in every such case; the same applies to the members of the Sangha.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a pāyattika offense.
There is no offense if she did not know it beforehand, if she accepted the words of another in good faith, if there was testimony from a bystander, or if she acted on the word of her parents.
If, after having received the precepts, one has doubts, the Buddha said:
"One should count the months of the pregnancy, count the intercalary months, and count all the fortnights of the *poṣadha* observances as years; if the full number is reached, it is permitted."
66. The Precept on Initiating the Four Kinds of Disputes.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
After the six groups of monks had settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, they later initiated it once again.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who therefore established this precept.
If a bhikṣu, whether knowing or not knowing that a dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, does not [report it], he commits no offense.

There are four kinds of disputes: disputes concerning speech (*vāda-vivāda*), disputes concerning accusations (*anuvāda-vivāda*), disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*), and disputes concerning legal matters (*kicca-vivāda*).
Having performed the confession according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s instruction,
should one again give rise to [the offense], it is a *pāyattika*.
If the confession is not fully articulated, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Aside from settling this dispute, if other quarrels or verbal altercations arise;
if a dispute has already arisen;
or if other persons, excluding the two assemblies, initiate a dispute—all such cases constitute a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
The same applies to the offense for a nun. There is no offense in the following cases:
if she was unaware beforehand;
If one observes [the object] but does not form a mental image;
or if the fact is actually so, such that one says "it was not observed well," etc.;
or if it was done in jest, or by mistake—there is no offense.
67. The Precept Against Agreeing to Travel with Robbers.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A large number of bhikṣus traveled to Vaiśālī.
A merchant, attempting to cross the frontier gate in secret without paying the king's tax, traveled as a companion to a bhikṣu.
He was seized by the gatekeepers and brought before the king; his crime merited the death penalty.
The king and the laity censured him.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept:
If a bhikṣu, whether knowing or not knowing that a formal agreement has not been made, [engages in the act], he does not commit an offense.

Regarding the companions of a thief: whether they have returned from committing a robbery or are about to depart, they make a pact to travel together along the same path. To "make a pact" means they agree together to go as far as a city or a village.
A "road" refers to any path between villages.
Even within a single village, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one travels along various paths between villages or travels along a single path, one commits an offense.
If one travels together for ten *li* in a desolate place where there are no villages and no defined boundaries, an offense is committed.

If one travels together halfway through a village, or less than ten *li*, or within a village, or if one makes preparations or agrees to travel but does not go, all such cases constitute a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).
The same applies to nuns for a common offense.

There is no offense if one travels together for safety to a destination, or if it is due to life-threatening danger, the influence of Brahmā, or the force of power; in these cases, there is no offense.
Sixty-eight: The precept against preaching that desire does not obstruct the Path in violation of the Sangha’s admonition.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A wrong view arose in Ariṣṭa, who said:
"I know that the Buddha taught that engaging in sexual desire does not obstruct the path."
When the bhikṣus admonished him with parables and he still did not relinquish [his position], they informed the Buddha.

After the Buddha had questioned him regarding his own statement, he ordered the Saṃgha to admonish him through a formal *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations), and then, having rebuked him, he established the precept.
If a bhikṣu speaks thus: "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha:
engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstructive dharma for the path."
That monk should admonish the other monk, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not speak such words; do not slander the Blessed One, for it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One."
"The Blessed One does not speak thus; by countless skillful means, the Blessed One has taught that the commission of sexual misconduct is a dharma that obstructs the path.
When those monks admonished this monk, he stubbornly persisted and would not relinquish his position. Those monks then admonished him up to three times so that he might abandon this matter.
If, after being admonished a second and third time, she abandons [the course], it is well;
if she does not abandon it, it is a *pāyattika*.
The same applies to the nuns as for the monks.
The remainder is as in the "Admonition Precept," with the only difference being the degree of gravity of the offense.
Sixty-nine: The precept concerning following a formal accusation against a bhikṣu.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Liṭha gave rise to evil views; when the Saṃgha admonished him and he would not relinquish them, the Buddha ordered that he be formally charged through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
The group of six monks provided him with his necessities and participated in the same formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*) as him.
Because a bhikṣu had raised this matter as a transgression, the Buddha reprimanded him and consequently established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu knows [the offense], or if he did not know it at first but later [realizes it], there is no violation."
A person who speaks thus says: "I have heard the World-Honored One teaching the Dharma that engaging in sexual misconduct is not an obstructive dharma.
Because he has not performed the formal act, if he is suspended, he has not yet been released from that suspension.
Thus, with such wrong views, he holds this perspective:
"I know that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is not a teaching that obstructs the path.
Yet he does not relinquish it; though the Saṃgha rebukes and exhorts him, he does not abandon his evil view.
There are two kinds of providing what is required: that which pertains to the Dharma and that which pertains to material wealth.
As for the Dharma, it consists of teaching the cultivation of higher virtue, mind, and wisdom, as well as study and the recitation of the scriptures.
As for material wealth, it consists of providing clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.
Common formal acts (*kamma*), the recitation of the *Poṣadha* together, and so forth.
Regarding dwellings for staying overnight, there are four types: those with walls on all four sides and completely covered and enclosed;
or those that are completely covered but not completely enclosed.
Or there may be total obstruction but not total concealment;
or there may be neither complete concealment nor complete obstruction.

Regarding speech: if a bhikṣu enters a house first and that person enters later, or if that person arrives first, or if they enter together, then for each instance of leaning against the side of the wall, he incurs an offense of falling [into a transgression].
A *pāyattika*. Nuns commit the same offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
If one does not know;
or if the house is entirely roofed with no openings on four sides, or with half-openings, or with few openings;
or if it is entirely enclosed with no roof, or a half-roof, or a small roof;
Or if it is half-covered, slightly covered, or in the open air;
or if one is ill, bound, or faces a threat to life or to the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya), there is no offense.
Seventieth: The precept concerning a śrāmaṇera who has been expelled.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Two śrāmaṇeras, Upananda’s disciples, engaged in unchaste conduct together and said to themselves:
"We have heard the Dharma from the Buddha:..."
"Engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the Path.

When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha ordered that a formal motion with three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) be made to admonish him; when he did not desist, he was expelled.
The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) then lured him away and took him in as their follower.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha rebuked them and established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has spoken thus:
'I have heard such a teaching from the Buddha...'"
"If one engages in sexual misconduct, it is not a factor that obstructs the path.
The bhikṣu should admonish this śrāmaṇera, saying:
"Do not slander the Blessed One; to slander the Blessed One is unwholesome."
The World-Honored One does not speak thus. Śrāmaṇera!
By means of countless skillful means, the World-Honored One has taught that sensual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
When that bhikṣu exhorts this śrāmaṇera and he persists in his refusal to relinquish it, that bhikṣu should exhort him up to three times in order to cause him to relinquish that matter.
If he relinquishes [the practice] after up to three admonitions, that is well.
If he does not relinquish it, that bhikṣu should say to this śrāmaṇera:
"From this day forward, you must not say, 'The Buddha is my World-Honored One,' nor may you follow other bhikṣus."
"Just as śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay with bhikṣus for two or three nights, you have no such right now.
You must leave, depart, and should not remain here."
If a bhikṣu acts out of ignorance, he commits no offense. Likewise, regarding a śrāmaṇera who has been expelled from the saṃgha:
"expulsion" refers to the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) carried out by the saṃgha to effect his exclusion.
And as for luring them away to be kept and raised— whether keeping them oneself or having others keep them—
"luring" means either doing it oneself or instructing another.
"Staying overnight together" is explained as above.
This is a *pāyattika*.
Nuns commit the same offense.
The exceptions are as stated above.
71. The Precept Against Rejecting Exhortations to Study.
When the Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī, a bhikṣu admonished Chanda in accordance with the Dharma, but Chanda spoke as follows:
"I will not train in this precept now; I shall instead consult other wise ones who uphold the Vinaya.
When a bhikṣu raised this transgression, the Buddha rebuked him and established the rule:
"If a bhikṣu, when other bhikṣus are admonishing him in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching..."
If one speaks thus: "I will not train in this precept now; I shall instead question other wise bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya," it is a pāyattika.
If one speaks but does not finish the statement, it is a duṣkṛta.
A nun commits an offense together with the Saṃgha.
If it is for the sake of training, she should pose difficult questions.

There is no offense if the one who offers the admonition is foolish and does not understand her words, saying, "You should go back and ask your upādhyāya or ācārya regarding study, inquiry, and the recitation of sūtras," provided that the facts are indeed as stated. There is no offense.
Seventy-two: Violating the Vinaya Precepts.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The bhikṣus gathered together to recite the Dharma and the Vinaya.
The group of six monks said to one another, "The bhikṣus have gathered together; since they are thoroughly proficient in reciting the Vinaya, they will surely censure us repeatedly.
They said, "Elders, what is the use of studying these trivial precepts?"
"One may recite up to thirteen matters.
Because the bhikṣus knew that the Dharma was declining, they reported the transgression to the Buddha, who then rebuked them and established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited—whether he himself is reciting the precepts, another is reciting the precepts, or when [the text] is being chanted—[acts in such a manner]."
He spoke these words: "Venerable Sir!
What is the use of reciting these minor precepts?
If one wishes to recite them, one should recite only the four pārājika offenses."
"If you must recite them, you should recite only the four matters and the thirteen matters; the rest need not be recited.
Why? Because when these precepts are being spoken, they cause people distress, shame, and doubt. To belittle and revile the precepts constitutes a *pāyattika* offense."
If it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
To disparage the *vinaya* is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
To disparage the *abhidharma* or other sūtras is a *duṣkṛta*.
The nuns commit the same offense.
There is no offense in cases such as saying: "First recite the Abhidharma, and afterwards recite the Vinaya," or likewise regarding other sūtras.
If there is one who is ill, [the rule is]: "One must recite the Vinaya only after having recovered";

"One should diligently seek skillful means to realize the four fruits of the śramaṇa within the Buddha-dharma, and only thereafter shall one recite the Vinaya," so as not to allow the extinction of the Dharma;
if one should speak erroneously—[in all such cases] it is permitted.
73. Fear of Being Accused: Preemptively Speaking of the Precepts.

When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, one member of the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks, while it was time for the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), became aware of his own transgressions. Fearing that they would be brought to light, he went first to a pure monk and said:
"I have only now learned that this Dharma is contained within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month; it has come down from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Because a bhikṣu had raised this matter as a transgression, the Buddha established this precept.
If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited—whether he is reciting them himself or another is reciting them—makes this statement:
"Only now do I know that this rule is contained in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*";
and if other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has sat through two or three such recitations of the precepts, let alone more;

If that bhikṣu is ignorant and lacks understanding, and he commits an offense, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma; furthermore, an additional offense of ignorance should be added, and he should be formally charged with a pāyattika.
If it is not so administered, it is a duṣkṛta.
He said: "Elder! You have gained no benefit; you have not attained it well."
"When you recite the precepts, you do not apply your mind with mindfulness, but instead contemplate with discursive thought;
you do not listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus and both ears.
Because of this ignorance, it is an *pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to nuns regarding the offense.
There is no offense in cases where one has not previously heard the detailed exposition and only now hears it for the first time;
or if it was spoken in jest; or if it was spoken by mistake—these are permitted.
74. The Precept on Regretting a Collective *Karmavācanā*.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
Trapuṣabhadra, who was managing the affairs of the Saṃgha, did not attend to external duties; consequently, his robes became worn and torn.
Later, when the monks obtained a precious robe, they offered it to him by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. The group of six monks later regretted this.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who rebuked them and established the precept:

"If a bhikṣu, after a formal ritual (*karman*) has been performed together, subsequently speaks thus: 'The bhikṣus act according to their personal friends; those who sit, rise, and converse with intimacy are merely following their own *upādhyāyas* and *ācāryas*.'"
Regarding "the property of the Saṃgha" and "the property of the monks," these are as explained above.
As for "property," it refers to robes, alms bowls, needle cases, sitting mats, and so forth, down to drinking vessels and water containers.
To give [such items] away constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one speaks without making it clear, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a nun, the offense is the same.
There is no offense if the matter is indeed so, and one gives monastic property to a relative or friend accordingly.
If spoken in jest or by mistake, both are permitted.
Seventy-five: The precept against giving consent [to another's offense].
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A large number of bhikṣus gathered to discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya.
The group of six bhikṣus said to one another, "Look at these bhikṣus; it seems they are performing a formal ritual (karmavācanā) against us," and they rose from their seats and departed.
A bhikṣu called out for someone to stop, yet the person continued on their way.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, he rebuked him and established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu, while the Saṃgha is performing a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa or a single formal act (karmavācanā)..."
While the legal proceedings have not yet been concluded, there are eighteen matters concerning the schism of the Saṃgha:
what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to what is spoken and what is not spoken.
If one has not granted their consent (*chanda*) but is engaged in affairs of the Saṃgha, affairs of a stūpa or monastery, or in attending to the sick, it is permitted for them to grant their consent.
If one rises and departs, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the legal proceedings have not yet concluded and one moves a foot outside the door, one commits a *pāyattika*.
If one foot remains inside the door and one makes an effort to leave but does not do so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is a *niḥpātya* offense.
There is no offense if one has given consent (*chanda*), or if one’s mouth is closed;

or if one is performing a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*); or if one departs without giving consent for the sake of causing harm to the Sangha, a stupa, a monastery, a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), a teacher (*ācārya*), or a fellow student. In these cases, it is permissible.
Seventy-six: The precept concerning regretting a formal consent (*chanda*) after having given it.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six [monks] feared being formally accused; thus, the six followed one another, finding no way to carry out their actions.

Later, while robes were being made, the Sangha summoned him to receive the *chanda* (consent). He immediately granted it, and the monks performed the formal act of *ukkhepanīya-kamma* (suspension) against that bhikkhu.
Subsequently, the group of six said, "I gave my consent regarding that matter."
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha, on that account, rebuked them and established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu, having given his consent (*chanda*), later regrets it and says:
'The *karmavācanā* you performed was contrary to the Dharma; the *karman* is not valid.'"
"If I grant my consent for that matter, and not for this one," constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If the statement is incomplete, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The nuns are equally culpable.
There is no offense if the matter was indeed so, and they performed an illegal *karmavācanā*.
If there was a mistake in addressing the parties involved, it is permitted.
Seventy-seventh: The precept against eavesdropping on the four types of disputes.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks listened to the quarreling bhikṣus and then reported it to others, causing the monastic community to be unable to settle the dispute.
When the monks reported this transgression, the Buddha, because of it, rebuked them and established a rule:

"If a monk, after having engaged in a dispute with other monks—there being four kinds of disputes, namely: through speech, through seeking [faults], through offenses, and through matters—" [he should not persist in that dispute]."
Regarding "listening to these words": one who speaks toward another is the speaker; one who listens is the listener.

To listen to another's speech means to eavesdrop on their conversation. Whether listening to those words by going from the path to the non-path, or from high to low, or conversely as stated above, it refers to going and hearing them.
A *pāyattika* offense.
If he does not hear it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he employs means intending to go but does not go, or if he makes an appointment to go together but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If two people converse together in a dark place, in a secluded place, or while walking ahead of one another, and they do not snap their fingers or cough to alert each other, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense in every instance.
The nuns commit the same offense as the monks.
There is no offense if they listen with the intention of knowing whether a *karmavācanā* is being performed that is unbeneficial or contrary to the Dharma.
Seventy-eight: The precept against striking a *bhikṣu*.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
One member of the group of six became enraged and struck one member of the group of seventeen; the one who was struck cried out loudly.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it in full detail.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu—whether with his hand, a stone, a staff, or other such means."
This constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Excluding the use of a staff, the hand, or a stone, if one prods with a door-key, a curved hook, the handle of a fly-whisk, or the handle of an incense burner, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies to nuns regarding offenses.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one has an illness that requires striking; if, while swallowing food, it is necessary to strike the spine; or if, when speaking together, one touches the other to make them hear because they cannot otherwise hear.

It is permitted if one lies down while sleeping with the body resting upon another, or if they touch one another while walking back and forth in meditation, or if the tip of a broom accidentally touches them while sweeping the ground.
79. The Precept on Striking Other Bhikṣus.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six bhikṣus struck the group of seventeen with their hands, and those who were struck raised their voices and cried out loudly.
The bhikṣus reported the transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu with his hand, it is a pāyattika."
If one strikes another with both hands, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one strikes with a door-key or similar object, it is all a *dukkaṭa*.
For *bhikṣuṇīs*, the offense is the same as for the *bhikṣus*.
There is no offense if there is a necessary reason to raise one's hand to ward off, beckon, or touch another.
Eighty: The Precept on Slandering Regarding Residual Offenses.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks, out of malice, slandered the group of seventeen monks with a groundless charge of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
When the monks reported this transgression, the Buddha rebuked them and established this precept:
"If a monk, out of malice, [accuses another] as described above with what is groundless."
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of slandering: it is a *pāyattika*.
Nuns commit the same offense. There is no offense in the following cases:
There are three cases where there is no offense: if one speaks the truth with the intent to cause repentance and does not slander;
or if it was spoken in jest; or if it was spoken by mistake.
81. The precept concerning entering the gates of a royal palace.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Lady Mallikā provided offerings to the Buddha and served him with faith; she exhorted the King to have confidence and joy, obtaining permission for the bhikṣus to enter the palace without hindrance.
When Kālodāyin arrived and entered the palace at the appointed time, the lady was sweeping the couch and accidentally exposed her body by losing her garment.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the precept:

"If a bhikṣu [should so act], regarding a Kṣatriya of the lineage of kings consecrated by water—the 'consecrated by water' being one for whom the waters of the great ocean and the right horn of a white ox are gathered to collect the seeds, which are placed upon a golden palanquin carried by various minor kings, while great Brahmins pour water over the crown of his head."
This refers to one of the Kṣatriya caste; because he is established as king in this manner, he receives that name.
If one of the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes is established in this same way, they are likewise called "Anointed" (abhiṣikta).
The king had not yet departed; the king had not yet departed, and the maiden had not yet returned to her original place.
The treasures—gold, silver, pearls, mother-of-pearl, agate, crystal, lapis lazuli, and shell-jewels—had not yet been concealed; the various precious necklaces and ornaments had not yet been put away.
If one enters and crosses the threshold of the palace gate, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is outside the threshold and one foot is inside, and one forms the intention to depart, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
Except for the king, if one enters the threshold of the dwellings of other minor local kings, wealthy elders, or noble families, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The same applies to nuns.
There is no offense if there is a formal announcement, if one has been invited or summoned, or if there are circumstances involving danger to life or to the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*).
82. The Precept on Taking Precious Objects.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Some non-Buddhists were traveling along a road; they stopped to rest and departed, having forgotten a thousand ounces of gold.
A bhikṣu saw it and took it away for him, returning it with gold.
[The owner] then said the gold was insufficient; the king adjudicated the case and punished him, confiscating the gold for the state.
The bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who then rebuked him and established this precept.
If a bhikṣu [touches] treasures such as gold, silver, pearls, amber, conch shells, agate, lapis lazuli, cowrie shells, or raw gold and silver.
As well as jeweled ornaments—those made of copper, iron, lead, tin, and white wax adorned with various gems.

Whether she holds them herself or instructs another to hold them, except when within a monastery, Vimalā (Vesākhamātā) removed her jeweled garments while listening to the Buddha’s teaching; she remembered the Dharma but forgot the clothes.
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha, "I request permission to pick it up so that it may not be lost and for the sake of its preservation.

At the time he was staying at a lodging, while traveling on the road, the bhikṣu stayed overnight at the house of a goldsmith; with the finished and unfinished gold pieces laid out before him, he remained awake throughout the entire night guarding them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Because it is for the sake of security, you should collect and store it away.
[If you do not,] it is a pāyattika offense."
The nuns commit the offense in the same manner as the monks.

If, within a monastery or at a lodging place, they take hold of precious objects or ornaments made of precious materials—whether taking them up themselves or instructing another to do so—they should maintain this thought:
"If there is an owner who recognizes it, let them take it."
If one obtains treasure at both locations, one should take hold of it, identify the characteristics of the bags or containers, and count how much there is.
If someone comes and asks for it, give it to them if they are a suitable recipient;
if they are not a suitable recipient, say, "I did not see it."

If one does not know the characteristics of the bag’s vessel, its lining, or its fastenings, and fails to examine whether it is square or round, new or old, it is a *pācittiya* offense (*kṣudrānukṣudra-āpatti*) in all such cases;
this applies only to these specific causes and conditions, and no others.
There is no offense in the following cases:
if it is within a monastery or a lodging, as in the aforementioned method of picking up and holding;
or if it concerns the ornaments for the adornment of a stūpa or temple, and one picks them up for the purpose of securing them—there is no offense in all such instances.
83. The Precept Against Entering a Village at an Improper Time.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Baddhananda entered a village at an improper time and won at dice with a householder.
Because the lay devotees were stingy and envious, they criticized and disparaged him.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu, regarding 'non-time'—that is, from the appearance of dawn until midday—" [should eat solid or soft food, it is a pācittiya offense].
"Improper time" refers to the period from after midday until the appearance of the dawn light.
Regarding "entering a village," there are four types of villages as described above.
Regarding "not informing a bhikṣu," the Buddha said that there are times when there are matters concerning the Saṃgha, the stūpa, or the monastery, or matters concerning the care of the sick.
"If one instructs a bhikṣu,
and if staying alone in a single room, one must entrust oneself to a neighboring room," this constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one first enters the village gate, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one foot has entered within, as well as in cases of preparatory effort (*prayoga*) or making a prior appointment (*samanvāhāra*), all constitute a *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies to nuns.
There is no offense if one is engaged in affairs for the Saṃgha, a stūpa, or the sick, having entrusted the matter to another bhikṣu;

or if the path passes through a village and one has made a formal announcement; or if one is summoned or invited; or if there are difficult circumstances such as threats to life or obstacles to the Brahma-faring. There is no offense in these cases.
84. The Precept on Exceeding the Size of a Bed.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
Kāḷudāyin, having foreknowledge that the Buddha would come along this road, immediately spread out a high and fine bed in the middle of the path and said:
"Look at my seat! the Buddha said.
"One should know that this foolish person harbors evil within."
Having assembled the Saṃgha and rebuked him, he established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu makes a cord bed or a wooden bed, the five types are as described above.
The legs must not exceed the height of eight fingers of the Tathāgata, except for the portion inserted into the socket of the frame."
Once the cutting is finished, if one exceeds [the prescribed limit], it is a *pāyattika*.
Whether one does it oneself or instructs another to do it, if it is completed and exceeds [the limit], one commits a *pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, or if one does it for another, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies to the nuns regarding the offense.
There is no offense if the height is made exactly eight finger-breadths, or less.
If another person gives [cotton], one may cut it and use it; this applies also to that which has been removed from a footstool.
Eighty-five: The precept concerning the use of *tūla* (cotton) for bedding.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks made mattresses stuffed with *tūla* cotton. Laypeople criticized them, saying, "They are killing living beings; they have no heart of compassion.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept to prohibit it.
If a bhikṣu [uses] *tūla* cotton, *śirīṣa* flower, willow flower, or *kaśa* reed flower—these are what is meant.
There are five types of storage for rope beds and wooden beds, as described above.
Regarding large and small bedding: for the purpose of sitting or lying down, if it is completed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Whether one does it oneself or instructs another to do so, it is as stated above.
The nuns are equally culpable.
There is no offense in cases identical to those explained above under the section on permitted conditions.
Eighty-six: The precept concerning the making of needle-cases from bone, ivory, or horn.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

There was a faithful artisan who, for the sake of a bhikṣu, made needle cases from bone, ivory, and horn; because of this, he neglected his trade and lacked food and clothing. People of the world criticized him, saying:
"He hoped to gain merit, but instead incurred calamity."
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, having carved or scraped it into shape, it is a pāyattika."
If one makes it oneself or instructs another to make it, the offense is established as described above.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if it is made of iron, copper, lead, tin, or white bronze; or if it is made of bamboo, wood, reeds, or śara grass for use as a needle case.

If one makes a head-piece for a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), a finial for a banner, a handle for an umbrella, or a finial for a ladle; if one wraps the cover or the ladle; if one makes a hook, a sweat-wiping blade, a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem), a toggle-knot, a spoon, a ladle, a robe-hanger, an ointment-stick for the eyes, a tongue-scraper, a toothpick, an ear-cleaner, a meditation weight, or a nose-pipe—for such things as these, there is no offense.
87. The Precept on Oversized Reclining Mats.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
It is the constant practice of all Buddhas that, unless invited, they tour the dwellings; seeing the monks' bedding spread out in the open air and defiled by impurities, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Even non-Buddhist seers who have renounced desire do not do such a thing.
It is permitted to make a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) for the purpose of covering one’s robes and bedding.
The group of six monks made them excessively large; when the other bhikṣus pointed out this fault, the Buddha consequently established the precept.
If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) for use while seated, it must be made according to the prescribed measurements. The measurement therein is:

two spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and one and a half spans in width. At that time, Kālodāyin’s body was large and his *niṣīdana* was small; he reported this to the Buddha, who then permitted it to be increased.
If it exceeds by more than half a *vitasti* in either width or length,
once the cutting is finished, it is a *pāyattika*. If both the width and length exceed [the limit],
whether they exceed individually or both together, if one makes it oneself or instructs another to make it, and it is completed, one commits a *pāyattika*.
If it is not completed, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one causes another to do it, whether it is completed or not, it is a duṣkṛta.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if [the cloth] is smaller, or if it is folded, or if another person obtains it for tailoring.
Eighty-eight: The precept concerning a patching cloth that exceeds the prescribed measure.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
If a bhikṣu suffers from an ulcer from which pus and blood flow out, defiling the monastic bedding,
he is permitted to cover the ulcer with a high-priced robe while wearing his undergarment (nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī).
When visiting the homes of laypeople, he should say, "I am ill," and should lift up his undergarment so that he may sit while covering the ulcer with this [robe].
The group of six monks made them excessively large. When the bhikṣus pointed out this fault, the Buddha consequently established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu makes a garment for covering sores—intended for use to cover the body when suffering from various types of sores or diseases—" [he shall make it according to the prescribed measure].
It should be made according to the proper measure;
herein, the measure is four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width.
If, after it has been cut, it exceeds these dimensions, it is a *pāyattika*.
If both [factors] are present and mutually deficient, whether one acts for oneself or instructs another, if it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one acts for another, whether it is completed or not, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For nuns and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if [the robe] is of the proper measure, or less than the proper measure, or if one obtains a finished garment and cuts it to the proper measure, or folds it to make it so.
Ninety-eight: The precept concerning rain-cloths exceeding the proper measure.
When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the mother of Viśākhā sent a rain-bathing robe. The Buddha said:
"It must not be divided; it shall be given to the senior monk."
"If there is a shortage, it shall be continued in the order of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the six groups of monks who made them excessively large, the bhikṣus reported the transgression, and the Buddha consequently established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe, it is for the purpose of wearing it while bathing in the rain."
It should be made according to the prescribed measure;
the measure herein is six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width.
If it exceeds these dimensions, having finished cutting it, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one acts oneself, instructs another, both do so, or there is mutual reduction; for a bhikṣuṇī, the allowance for extenuating circumstances is the same as in the preceding precept.
Ninety: The precept on robes exceeding the prescribed measure.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

Nanda was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha; when the bhikṣus saw him from afar, they thought it was the Buddha coming to welcome them, but upon reaching him, they realized it was not so, and each felt ashamed.
The Buddha ordained that Nanda should wear black robes.
The group of six monks made robes equal in size to the Buddha’s or even larger than his. When the bhikṣus reported this excess, the Buddha consequently established a precept:
If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to the Tathāgata’s or makes one exceeding that size, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe among these: it is nine spans (vitasti) in length and six spans in width; this is called the measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe.
If the width and length are both according to the measure, yet one or the other is not according to the measure, in either case there is an offense.
The cases of making it oneself, instructing another to do so, or having a nun make it, are all as explained above.
There is no offense if one obtains a finished garment from another and cuts it to the proper dimensions; nor is there an offense if it is folded double.
Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable sirs:
"In this matter, are you pure?
This is asked three times. "Venerable sirs!"
In this matter, we are pure, for we remain silent.
Thus shall this be upheld.

Venerable sirs! These four *pārajitikā-dharma* (dharmas requiring confession) are recited every half-month and have come down from the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*.
1. The precept concerning taking food from a nun who is not a relative within a village.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the world was in a famine and grain was expensive; there were countless people dying of hunger.

The nun Utpalavarṇā, having put on her robes and taken up her alms bowl, entered the city to beg for food; however, for three consecutive days she gave [all the food] to the bhikṣus, and consequently remained starving by the roadside, lying down with her face buried in the mud.
Laypeople criticized and disparaged them.
The bhikṣus reported these transgressions to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu enters a village and, from one who is not a relative, [acts] as described above."
For a bhikṣuṇī, if she is not ill, it is also as stated above.
Taking food with one’s own hand regarding the two kinds of food is also as stated above.
Regarding "eating," this bhikṣuṇī should confess her transgression to another bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
I have committed a censurable act, which ought not to have been done; I now repent before the Venerable Sir!
This is called the procedure for repentance.
If one receives it with one's own hand, there is an offense for every swallow.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if she receives food from a relative bhikṣuṇī, or if she is ill.

If it is placed on the ground, if it is handed over by another person, if it is given within a monastery, if it is given outside the village, or if it is given within a nunnery—receiving it in such ways does not constitute an offense.
2. The precept against eating food directed by a nun.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A large number of bhikṣus, together with the group of six, were eating at the home of a layperson.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs sought out soup and rice, bypassing their proper order to give them to the group of six bhikṣus, saying, "Give this soup to him; give this rice to him.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established a precept.
If a bhikṣu goes to the house of a layperson where there are both men and women,
and they provide food as described above,
and if among them a bhikṣuṇī directs [the host], saying, "Give soup to so-and-so; give rice to so-and-so," that bhikṣu should speak to that bhikṣuṇī as follows:
“Sister, please stop for a moment; wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating.

If not even a single bhikṣu says to that bhikṣuṇī, “Sister, please stop for a moment; wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating,” then that bhikṣu should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
“Venerable sir!...”
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done; I now repent before the Venerable One!
This is called the method of repentance (*deśanā-dharma*).
If one eats without having been reproved, one commits an offense with every swallow.
Nigirā. There is no offense if one says:
"Sister, please stop for a moment; wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating."
If a nun acts as a donor herself;
or if a donor provides food and instructs the nun to manage it;
or if she does not intentionally show partiality toward this person or that person—she commits no offense.
3. The Precept on Accepting Food from a Family Under Training.

When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, a householder and his wife both attained the vision of the Truths (dṛṣṭisatyāni); they had nothing for which they felt attachment or regret, even unto their own flesh.
As the offerings became numerous, their food and clothing were completely exhausted.
Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, and the bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha.
The Buddha ordered that a formal proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) be made to prohibit it; later, when they became wealthy again, he then established this precept.
If the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a family under protection has already been performed, the Saṃgha shall grant permission through a motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
As for "family," it is as described above.
If a bhikṣu goes to such a family under protection without having been previously invited, or if he was previously invited, his going is permitted.
If one is not ill, it is permitted for a sick bhikṣu to accept food from such a household.
Whether the food is received directly by hand, placed on the ground to be given, or provided by another person, it is permitted.
One who eats [such food] should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have committed a censurable act that ought not to have been done; I now repent my transgression before you, Venerable sir!
This is called the procedure for repentance.
If one receives it with one's own hand, there is an offense for every swallow.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if she was previously invited, if she is ill, if she takes it after placing it on the ground, if she receives it from another person, or if she has already received the food after the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya*) has been resolved. In all such cases, there is no offense.
4. The precept regarding receiving food in a terrifying forest hermitage.
The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Śrāvastī.
A woman from the city brought food as an offering, but on the road, she was harassed by bandits.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should inform them so that they may know," and he then established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu stays in an araṇya (wilderness) five hundred bows' distance from a village—this being according to the cubit measurement used in the kingdom of Camara."

In remote places where there is suspicion and fear, such as the apprehension of bandits and thieves—if a bhikṣu dwells in such a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) and has not previously informed the donor, the Buddha said:
"He should tell the women, 'Do not go out; there is the danger of bandits on the road.'"
If one does not accept food outside the monastery, or has already left the city, one should say:
"Do not go into the monastery, for there are dangers from bandits on the road."
Within the saṃghārāma, if one is not ill and yet someone intentionally brings food, it is permitted for the sick person to receive it.
If one receives food with one's own hand, or if there is a donor who places the food on the ground, or instructs another to give it; [in these cases, it is likewise permitted].
Regarding the offense of eating: this bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have committed a censurable act that ought not to have been done; I now confess my transgression to you, Venerable sir!"
This is called the method for repentance.
Regarding Niggaṇṭha:
there is no offense if she comes to receive instructions or listen to the Dharma, and one personally eats while having her accept [the food].
Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable sirs:
"Is there purity herein? This is asked three times.
"Venerable sirs!"
In this matter, we are pure, because we remain silent.
Thus shall this be upheld. Venerable sirs!
These are the various *śaikṣa-dharmas*, recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
First: the precept regarding wearing the *nirvāṇaka* (inner robe) in a neat and orderly manner.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks wore their lower robes (nirvāṇasaka) in a disheveled manner. Consequently, a lay devotee criticized them, saying:
"They are like those who perform jests and comic recitations at festivals, or like kings and great ministers."
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently rebuked them and established a precept.
Regarding the rule that one's robe must be properly adjusted and not worn in a disordered manner:
the phrase "below the robe" refers to having the fastening belt tied below the navel.
The "high" style has the hem level with the knees;
the "elephant trunk" style has one corner hanging down in front;
the "tāla-leaf" style has two corners hanging down in front.
"Fine pleats" refers to the gathered folds encircling the waist.
When putting on the *nirvāṇasaṅghāṭī*, if one wears it unevenly intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession;
because it was done intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper decorum (*anācāra*).
If it was not done intentionally, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For the four assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
This principle applies to all instances of offenses established in the subsequent sections as well.
Regarding the *śikṣākaraṇīya* rules, there is no offense in the following cases:
if an ulcer develops at the navel, one may wear [the garment] below it; or...
If there is a sore on the knee or the ankle, one may wear it high.
There is no offense if this is done within a monastery, outside a village, while working, or while walking on a path.
2. The precept on wearing the three robes in a neat and orderly manner.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks wore their robes in a disheveled manner. When an elder saw this, he criticized them:
"He claims for himself, 'I know the True Dharma,' yet what True Dharma is there in such a person!
His robes are not worn evenly; he is no different from a layperson.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who, by contemplating the three periods of time, established this precept.
One should wear the three robes in a neat and orderly manner; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
Regarding what is not neat:
"wearing them low" means they hang down past the elbows and expose the ribs.
The "high" [robe] has its corners extending above the ankles;
the "elephant-trunk" style has one corner hanging down in front;
the "tāla-leaf" style has both corners hanging down in front while the back is gathered up and raised high.
Regarding "fine pleating": having finished pleating, one applies the border.
There is no offense in cases such as when there is a sore on the shoulder or arm, or when wearing it low; these are exceptions as previously specified.
Third, the precept concerning entering the homes of laypeople with arms crossed over the back.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks walked into the houses of laypeople with their robes tucked up behind their backs. A householder criticized them, saying:
"They have no sense of shame; they are just like kings, ministers, and members of the householder class."
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha rebuked them and established a precept:
one must not fold the robe over the shoulders, nor fold it over the left or right shoulder.
This applies when entering the houses of laypeople or entering a village.
Regarding the *śikṣākarani*:
there is no offense if one has a sore or illness on the side of the ribs, or if one is within a monastery, or if one is traveling on a road, or if one is engaged in manual labor.
4. One must not sit in the house of a layperson with one’s robe tucked over both shoulders; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
5. The precept concerning sitting in the house of a layperson with the robe wrapped around the neck.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks entered the homes of laypeople with their robes wrapped around their necks.
The householders complained, saying, "They look like householder elders.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and the Buddha rebuked them and established a precept.
One must not wrap the robe around the neck and gather all the corners of the robe over the shoulder when entering the house of a layperson; this is a *śikṣākarani*.
There is no offense if one is ill, has sores on the shoulder or arm, or if it is within a monastery, outside a village, while working, or while traveling on a road.
6. One must not sit in the house of a layperson with a robe wrapped around the neck; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
7. The precept against covering one’s head while in the house of a layperson.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople with their heads covered by robes; a householder criticized them, saying, "What kind of True Dharma is this?
They cover their heads like thieves."
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported the transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept:
one must not cover the head, whether with tree leaves, fragments of material, or by using a robe to cover it.
Entering the house of a layperson is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
There is no offense if one is ill, or suffering from cold, or has a sore on the head, or runs with the head covered due to the two dangers of life or the *brahmacarya* (the religious life).
8. One must not sit with one’s head covered in the house of a layperson; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
9. The precept against skipping while walking in the house of a layperson.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople by leaping about; the householders criticized them, saying, "How shameless!
They enter the rooms like crows and sparrows."
The monks reported this transgression, and the Buddha, because of it, rebuked them and established a rule:
"One must not skip along or leap with both feet while entering the house of a layperson; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense."

There is no offense in cases where one has an illness; or is being beaten by others; or there are bandits; or there are wild beasts; or there are thorns; or one crosses a ditch or a moat, or leaps across mud.
10. One must not sit in the house of a layperson by jumping over seats; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
11. The precept against squatting while sitting in the house of a layperson.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A lay devotee invited the monks to his residence to partake of a meal.
The group of six monks squatted; as they sat side by side, their hands touched one another, causing them to fall over backward and expose their bodies.
The lay devotee spoke with reproach:
“[He is] shameless!
His naked appearance resembles that of a Brahmin.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently rebuked him and established a precept.
One must not sit squatting inside the house of a layperson, whether on the ground or upon a bed, with the buttocks not touching the ground.
This is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense.

There is no offense in cases where one is ill, or has sores around the buttocks, or when there is something to be given, or when performing a prostration, or when confessing, or when receiving instruction.
12. The precept against entering the houses of laypeople with hands on the hips.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople walking with their hands on their hips, whereupon a householder criticized them, saying:
"A śramaṇa claims for himself, 'I know the True Dharma,' yet he stands with his hands on his hips like a man who has recently married and attained his ambition, acting with arrogance and license.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently rebuked him and established a rule.
One must not cross one's arms over the waist or clasp the elbows behind the back;
this is because [it is a transgression]. When entering the house of a layperson while walking, it is a *śikṣāpada* offense.
There is no offense in cases where one is ill, has an ulcer arising beneath the ribs, is within a monastery, is outside a village, is engaged in work, or is traveling on a road.
13. One must not rest the elbows on the hips, as this obstructs the neighboring bhikṣu.
When sitting in the house of a layperson, this is a śikṣāpada.
14. The precept regarding swaying the body while entering the homes of laypeople.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks swayed their bodies as they entered the homes of laypeople, whereupon a householder criticized them, saying:
"Without shame!
You sway your body like a king or a great minister.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and the Buddha, because of it, rebuked them and established a precept.
One must not walk with the body swaying, nor with the body twisting to the left or right, nor walking with a hurried gait.
To enter the house of a layperson while doing so constitutes a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
Or they may fall ill;
or they may be struck by others, twisting their bodies to avoid the blow;
or they may be gored by a vicious beast, or encounter a carrying-spit, twisting their bodies to avoid it.
Fifteenth: One must not sway the body while walking or sitting in the house of a layperson; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
If one crosses a ditch by swaying the body, or puts on robes and looks to see if they are neat and orderly [in such a manner], it constitutes an offense. *Śikṣākaraṇīya*.
16. The precept against swinging the arms while walking into the homes of laypeople.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks swung their arms as they entered the homes of laypeople, whereupon a householder criticized them, saying:
“Without shame!
You swing your arms like a king or a householder!
The bhikṣu reported this transgression, and the Buddha rebuked him and established a rule.
One must not walk with arms swinging, nor walk with arms dangling forward and backward.
Entering the house of a layperson constitutes a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
Or there may be illness;
or when struck by others, one raises a hand to ward it off;
or when fierce beasts or those carrying spears approach, one raises a hand to ward them off.
Seventeenth: One must not cross a canal by swimming;
one may call out to companions with the hand.
Furthermore, one must not walk with swinging arms or sit with them dangling while in the residence of a layperson. This is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
18. The precept against entering the houses of laypeople with the body exposed.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople without properly covering their bodies, and the householders criticized them, saying:
"The clothing he wears does not properly cover his body, like that of a Brahmin.
When a bhikṣu reported this, the Buddha, because of it, rebuked him and established a precept:
"One should enter the houses of laypeople with the body well-covered; if one is in a village, the body must not be exposed in various places."
Śikṣākaraṇī: There is no offense if one is ill, or if one is bound, or if the wind blows the robe away from the body.
Nineteen: To sit in the house of a layperson while properly covering the body is a śikṣākaraṇī.
20. The Precept on Looking Around When Entering the Houses of Laypeople.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks looked around left and right as they entered the houses of laypeople. A householder criticized them, saying:
"Like a thief. The Buddha, because a bhikṣu had raised this transgression, rebuked him and established a precept:
one must not look left and right or gaze about here and there while in a village.
Entering the house of a layperson: a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
There is no offense in cases where one is ill; or [other such circumstances].
Or looking up at the sun, the time, or the seasons;

or when there is danger from Māra or Brahmā, seeking an opportunity on the left or right to flee—(21) one must not sit in the house of a layperson while looking around to the left or right; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.
22. The Precept on Loud Voices in the Houses of Laypeople.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople shouting loudly. A householder criticized them, saying:
"Just like Brahmins who lack a sense of shame and have no true Dharma," the Buddha rebuked and established a rule because a bhikṣu had pointed out their faults.

Regarding entering the houses of laypeople in silence: "In this regard, those who are not silent" refers to those who raise their voices and shout loudly, or those who give instructions, or those who call out loudly while offering food.
Regarding the *śikṣākaraṇīya* rules,
there is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill;
If one is deaf and does not hear, one must give instructions in a loud voice;
if one is giving food in a loud voice;
or if, during the two calamities of life or Brahmā, one runs away while shouting loudly.
23. Sitting silently in the house of a layperson is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
24. The precept regarding joking and laughing in the house of a layperson.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The group of six entered the houses of laypeople while laughing and joking; the householders criticized them, saying:
"How shameless! You laugh and joke like monkeys; what true Dharma can there be in this!"
The monks reported this transgression, and the Buddha, because of it, rebuked them and established a rule:
"One must not laugh with the teeth exposed in a playful manner.
Entering the house of a layperson while laughing in this way constitutes a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense."
There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if one’s lips are painful and one does not cover the teeth; or if one smiles out of joy while recollecting the Dharma. Twenty-five:
One must not sit in the house of a layperson laughing or joking; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
26. The Precept Against Accepting Food Without Due Attention.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A lay devotee invited the Saṃgha to partake of a meal offering.
The group of six monks ate without mindfulness, casting away the soup and rice.
A layperson criticized them, saying:
"These śramaṇas have no sense of moderation; they receive with such greed as if it were a time of high grain prices."
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently rebuked them and established a rule:
"To eat with improper attention— that is, to discard the soup and rice while eating—
is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense."
There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; or when, because the bowl is small, one discards rice while eating, or it falls back onto the table.
Twenty-seven: The precept against receiving food that overflows the bowl.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A householder invited the Saṃgha, but the group of six monks received food until their bowls overflowed, causing them to spill the soup and rice.
The householder criticized them, saying:
"Without shame and without satiety, they are like hungry ghosts greedily devouring more.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and consequently, the Buddha censured them and established the precept.
"The bowl should be level" means that one should not let the bowl overflow.
Receiving food [in this manner] constitutes a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense.
There is no offense if one is ill at the time, or if the bowl is small, or if the food falls onto the table.
Twenty-eighth: The precept against receiving soup until the bowl overflows.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A householder prepared an offering, but the group of six monks took such an excessive amount of rice that there was no room left for the soup.
The householder criticized them, saying:
"Like a starving person greedily devouring food.
When a bhikṣu pointed out this fault, the Buddha, on that account, rebuked him and established a rule:
one should receive soup in a bowl level with its rim; otherwise, it overflows and spills, causing defilement.
Śikṣākaraṇīya: There is no offense if one is ill at the time, or if the bowl is too small and the food falls onto the table, or if one receives the food equally.
Twenty-nine: The precept against receiving food unequally.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A householder prepared an offering and personally served the food.
Having himself set down the rice, he went inside to fetch the soup; when he returned, the rice had already been finished.
Having given him the soup, he went back to take rice; when he returned, the rice was gone and the soup was finished.
He was ridiculed as being like a starving person.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and consequently, the Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.
When eating soup, rice, and other foods, if they are not equal— that is, when the rice is finished while the soup remains—
it is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*. There is no offense in the following cases:
Or there may be illness;
or if one specifically requires soup and not rice, or likewise requires rice;
or if the time for the meal is about to pass; or in the event of the two perils of life or the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya)—those who eat quickly in such cases are permitted.
30. The Precept Against Taking Food Out of Order.
When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a lay devotee prepared an offering and personally served the food. The group of six monks took their food out of order.
A layperson criticized him, saying:
"He is never satisfied, just like a pig, a dog, an ox, a donkey, a camel, or a crow.
The bhikṣu reported this transgression, and the Buddha, because of it, rebuked him and established a precept.
One should eat in proper sequence; if one does not eat in sequence, it means taking food from various places within the bowl to eat.
This is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*. There is no offense in the following cases:
There may be those who are ill;
or those suffering from hot rice, who pick out the cool portions;
or if the time for the meal is about to pass; or in the event of the two perils of life or the Brahma-faring life—one may eat quickly.
31. The Precept on Scooping Food from the Alms Bowl.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A householder prepared an offering and served the food with his own hands.
The group of six monks, while receiving food, would tip their bowls to look at the empty space within them.
A householder criticized them, saying:
"You do not tire of receiving food; you are like oxen, donkeys, horses, camels, pigs, and dogs."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who consequently censured them and established the precept:
One must not scoop food from the center of the bowl toward its edges, nor scoop from the center of the bowl down to the bottom while eating; this is a śaikṣa-dharma.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill;
or if suffering from the heat of food, one opens it to allow it to cool.
If the time for the meal is about to pass, or if there is a double danger involving life or the Brahma-faring, one may quickly cut open [the food] and eat from within.
Thirty-second: The precept against seeking food for oneself.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
When the lay devotee prepared an offering, the group of six monks went to him personally to solicit food as if they were starving.
The lay devotee criticized them, saying:
"How can there be any True Dharma!"
"He accepts food without satiety.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and the Buddha, because of it, rebuked him and established a rule:
except when ill, one may seek food for oneself only when there is illness.
One must not seek soup or rice for oneself; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
There is no offense if one is ill.
Whether it be for the sake of others, or others acting for one's own sake,
or that which is obtained without being sought.
33. The Precept on Covering Soup with Rice.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

A householder prepared an offering, and the group of six monks received the soup. When the householder recognized them, he took the soup for them; the monks then covered the soup with rice from behind.
A lay devotee criticized him, saying:
"To receive and take without satiety is like a starving man; how can there be the True Dharma!
The bhikṣu reported this transgression, and the Buddha, because of it, rebuked him and established a precept.
If one covers the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more, it is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense.
There is no offense if one is ill.
34. The precept against looking at one’s neighbor with disdain: if invited to a meal, or when soup is required, or at times when rice is required.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A householder prepared a meal;
the group of six monks received only a small portion, while their fellow monks received large portions. They said to the householder:
"You have now invited the Saṃgha for the Pravāraṇā ceremony; however, how much may you give?
The householder has his preferences. He replied:
"We shall give it. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha,
who consequently established the precept.
One must not look into the bowl of the person sitting beside them; "looking into it" means looking to see who has more or less.
[If one does so] while eating, it is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense.

There is no offense if the person sitting beside them is ill, or if they have poor eyesight, and one looks for the sake of seeing whether they can obtain food or not, whether it is pure or impure, or whether it has been accepted or not yet accepted.
If one has an illness oneself, it is permitted.
Thirty-five: The precept against eating with the bowl unsecured.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
When a lay devotee provided food, the group of six monks accepted it and, looking around left and right, unconsciously allowed their neighbors to take their bowls and hide them.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established a precept.
One should eat with the thought of being mindful of the bowl, meaning one should not look left or right.
This is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*. There is no offense in the following cases:
At times there may be illness;
or if the eyesight of one's neighbor is dim, one should employ the aforementioned expedient;
or one may observe the time of day.
Or when one wishes to escape from the two dangers of Māra and Brahmā, looking around to the left and right.
Thirty-six: The Precept Against Large Mouthfuls of Food.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
When a lay devotee provided an offering, the group of six monks ate in such large mouthfuls that their mouths could not accommodate them.
The lay devotee criticized them, saying:
"You know no moderation; you are like pigs, dogs, camels, donkeys, oxen, crows, and birds."
The bhikṣus reported this matter, and the Buddha consequently established a precept:
One must not take a mouthful of food that is too large, such that it cannot be contained within the mouth.
This is a śikṣākaraṇīya.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill;
if the time for the meal is about to pass; or if one eats quickly due to the two difficulties of life-threatening danger or the threat of violating the Brahma-faring life.
Thirty-seven: The precept against gaping the mouth wide while waiting for food.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a lay devotee prepared an offering; however, before the food had arrived, the bhikṣus gaped their mouths wide open.
The layperson scoffed, saying:
"Shameless and insatiable!
You are like pigs, dogs, camels, oxen, and donkeys."
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and the Buddha, because of it, rebuked them and established a rule:
one must not open one’s mouth wide in anticipation of food; one must not open the mouth wide beforehand before the morsel of rice has even arrived.
Regarding the *śikṣākaraṇīya* rules:
there is no offense if one is at times afflicted by such an illness;
Or when the day was nearly over, and there were difficulties such as those involving the Brahmā-world or the life-force, one would eat very quickly.
Thirty-eight: The precept against speaking with food in the mouth.

These seven principles for the settlement of disputes are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Whenever a dispute arises among the bhikṣus, it should be immediately settled.
The Buddha said:
"There are four types of disputes:
disputes concerning speech, disputes concerning investigation, disputes concerning offenses, and disputes concerning legal matters."

A dispute concerning speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*) is settled by two means: the *pratyakṣavinaya* (settlement in the presence) and the *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti* (majority decision). A dispute concerning investigation (*anveṣaṇa-adhikaraṇa*) is settled by four means:

the *pratyakṣavinaya*, the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection), the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer insane), and the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (settlement according to the nature of the offense).

The *adhikaraṇa* of offenses (*āpatti*) is extinguished by three methods: settlement in the presence of the parties (*sammukhavinaya*), confession (*pratijñākāraka*), and the "covering with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*).
The *adhikaraṇa* of matters (*vastu*) is extinguished by all [seven] methods of settlement.
These three types of *adhikaraṇa* are each divided into three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—thus clarifying nine varieties in total.

The single category of *vastu-araṇa* (dispute over matters) passes through the three aforementioned types of disputes (*vivāda*, *anuvāda*, and *āpatti-araṇa*), being divided into nine grades according to their respective proportions.
It should correspond to the three or five types present before one, thereby extinguishing the superior, middling, and inferior grades.
